  No High-severity findings. The implementation stays within the requested
  skeleton scope, matches the documented Flask architecture, and doesn't
  introduce disallowed dependencies or premature MVP functionality (no DB, CRUD,
  status lifecycle, or reference-data logic present).

  Medium

  wsgi.py hardcodes debug=True unconditionally.
  if __name__ == "__main__":
      app.run(debug=True)
  This isn't gated by config or an environment variable, so debug mode
  (Werkzeug's interactive debugger + reloader) is always on for anyone running
  this entry point. architecture.md frames Phase 1 as intended to run locally,
  so risk is low today, but a hardcoded debug=True is a habit worth avoiding
  before it's forgotten later (e.g. app.run(debug=app.config.get("DEBUG", 
  False)), sourced from an env var). Recommend fixing before it becomes
  established pattern, though not blocking for this skeleton commit.

  Low

  - Unnecessary deferred import in the factory. src/job_hub/__init__.py imports
  main_bp inside create_app() rather than at module top level. routes.py has no
  import back on job_hub, so there's no circular-import reason for the deferral
  — it's indirection without benefit. Harmless, but a top-level import would be
  simpler and equally correct.
  - Config.SECRET_KEY falls back to the literal "dev". Currently inert (no
  sessions, flash, or CSRF-protected forms use it yet), so it's not exploitable
  today, but a hardcoded default secret is worth flagging so it isn't silently
  carried into a context where it matters without deliberate reconsideration.
  - No test exercises the create_app(config=...) override path. test_factory.py
  only calls create_app() with defaults, so the config or Config branch is
  untested. Minor completeness gap, not a defect — there's no alternate config
  object yet to meaningfully test against.

  Checklist confirmations (no issues found)

  - Architecture compliance: Flask + Jinja templates + CSS only, no SQLite/ORM
  code — correctly deferred per architecture.md.
  - Dependencies: pyproject.toml unchanged from documented Flask/pytest
  baseline; no new packages added.
  - Factory/blueprint structure: create_app() factory pattern and main_bp
  blueprint registration are structurally correct.
  - Selectors: id="home-page" and id="main-content" are stable, meaningful, and
  appropriately scoped for future Selenium use, per NFR-006/testability
  guidance.
  - Test quality: Assertions check actual behavior (blueprint registration,
  route status, rendered content) rather than trivial truisms — consistent with
  test-strategy.md's "Flask Application Testing" level.
  - Scope creep: No CRUD, persistence, or status-lifecycle logic present.
  - Git hygiene: .pytest_cache/, __pycache__/, and *.egg-info/ are generated on
  disk but correctly excluded by the existing .gitignore; nothing generated is
  staged.

● Approach and open physical-schema decisions

  Approach: Pure sqlite3 stdlib, no ORM. A single src/job_hub/schema.sql holds
  all DDL (tables, indexes, triggers, seed data); src/job_hub/db.py provides a
  connect() helper (enables PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON and sqlite3.Row on every
  connection), Flask g-scoped get_db()/close_db(), an idempotent init_db(), and
  a flask init-db CLI command, wired into create_app() via db.init_app(app). I
  validated the full schema against a scratch in-memory database before touching
  the project (FK enforcement, uniqueness, CHECK constraints, and STRICT-typed
  compensation columns all behaved as expected).

  Decisions the architecture deliberately left open, now resolved and documented
  in a new ADR:

  - Timestamp convention: all timestamps stored as TEXT ISO-8601 UTC with
  millisecond precision and Z suffix (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ), generated via
  SQLite's strftime(..., 'now') (UTC by default). application_date is date-only
  (YYYY-MM-DD), matching its documented semantics. created_at/last_updated_at
  are DB-generated (DEFAULT + AFTER UPDATE trigger per table) so the "maintained
  automatically" requirement doesn't depend on future application code
  remembering to set them.
  - employment_type value set: architecture explicitly defers this. I chose
  FULL_TIME, PART_TIME, CONTRACT, TEMPORARY (matching the MVP field
  description's examples).
  - LOCATION nullability/uniqueness with missing components: city,
  state_province, country are each individually nullable, but I added a CHECK
  requiring at least one non-blank component — this isn't literally spelled out,
  but it directly enforces the architecture's explicit "unknown location is a
  null FK, not a placeholder location" principle and prevents fully-empty
  degenerate rows. Flagging this inference explicitly since it's the one
  constraint I added beyond directly-stated rules. Equivalence/reuse uniqueness
  uses a normalized expression index treating missing components consistently
  (coalesce(...,'')).
  - STATUS terminal flags: OFFER treated as non-terminal (still awaiting
  applicant decision); ACCEPTED, REJECTED, WITHDRAWN, CLOSED are terminal.
  display_order 1–8 follows the architecture's listed sequence.
  - Numeric enforcement: used SQLite STRICT tables (supported — library version
  3.46.1) so compensation columns genuinely reject non-numeric values at write
  time, directly satisfying "shall not rely on a numeric-looking column
  declaration alone."
  - Initialization trigger point: schema/seed initialization is explicit (flask 
  init-db or calling job_hub.db.init_db() directly), not run automatically
  inside create_app(). This keeps plain create_app() calls (used by the existing
  factory/home-route tests) from silently touching a real database file, while
  remaining trivially compliant with "ordinary startup shall not reset data"
  since nothing currently reads/writes the DB at request time. This will need
  revisiting once CRUD routes exist and require guaranteed schema presence.

  Summary

  Files created:
  - src/job_hub/schema.sql — DDL for all six entities, expression-based unique
  indexes for normalized company/source/location equivalence, CHECK constraints,
  AFTER UPDATE triggers for last_updated_at, and idempotent STATUS seed data.
  - src/job_hub/db.py — connect() (enables PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON + sqlite3.Row
  on every connection), Flask g-scoped get_db()/close_db(), init_db(), and a
  flask init-db CLI command.

  documenting the timestamp convention and other physical-schema decisions.

  - src/job_hub/__init__.py — sets a default DATABASE config path under
  app.instance_path, ensures the instance folder exists, and calls
  db.init_app(app).

  Schema/constraint decisions (detailed rationale in the ADR): TEXT ISO-8601 UTC
  timestamps (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ) via DB-generated defaults + triggers;
  application_date as date-only TEXT; employment_type =
  FULL_TIME/PART_TIME/CONTRACT/TEMPORARY; LOCATION components individually
  nullable but a CHECK bars a fully-empty row; normalized-equivalence unique
  indexes for company/source/location; STRICT tables so compensation columns
  genuinely reject non-numeric writes; OFFER seeded as non-terminal,
  ACCEPTED/REJECTED/WITHDRAWN/CLOSED as terminal, display_order 1–8; DB
  initialization is explicit (flask init-db), not automatic on create_app().

  Tests added (17, in tests/test_db.py): schema creation (all six tables
  present), status seeding and ordering, idempotent re-initialization preserving
  existing data, FK enforcement, normalized uniqueness (company, location)
  including case/whitespace insensitivity, blank-name rejection, location
  placeholder rejection, (application_id, effective_at) uniqueness, compensation
  min≤max, compensation-basis-required, non-numeric compensation rejection
  (STRICT typing), invalid work_arrangement rejection,
  created_at/last_updated_at population and update-trigger behavior, and
  isolated-database usage via a Flask app context.

  pre-existing factory/route tests, unaffected.

  Intentionally deferred: CRUD routes/forms, creation transactions, duplicate
  detection, reference-data creation workflows, status-change workflows,
  archive/restore, search/filter/sort/pagination, and Selenium tests — none of
  this was touched, per scope. Also deferred: automatic schema initialization at
  ordinary app startup (currently explicit via flask init-db) — flagged in the
  ADR as a decision to revisit once CRUD routes exist.

  One incidental note: running create_app() creates an empty instance/ directory
  as a normal Flask side effect (no database file, since initialization stays
  explicit). It's untracked and invisible to git (empty dirs aren't tracked),
  and the .sqlite3 file it would eventually hold is already covered by the
  existing .gitignore pattern, so no further action was needed there.

● Review Summary

  Verified against the docs and empirically tested the implementation (temp
  databases only, no repo files modified). All 21 tests pass. No High-severity
  findings — the six tables, relationships, FK enforcement, and core constraints
  are correctly implemented, and no scope creep or SQL-injection surface exists
  in this slice.

  Medium

  1. trim() in the blank-text and location-placeholder CHECK constraints only 
  strips ASCII spaces, not tabs/newlines. Confirmed empirically: INSERT INTO 
  company (name) VALUES ('\t\t') succeeds — the tab-only value passes CHECK 
  (trim(name) <> ''). The same gap lets a LOCATION row with city = '\t' (all
  other components NULL) pass the "at least one real component" check. SQLite's
  single-argument trim() only removes the literal space character (0x20) by
  default. This falls short of the architecture's "insignificant leading or
  trailing whitespace" language for company/source/status names and location
  components. Recommend either an extended trim(x, 
  char(9)||char(10)||char(13)||char(32)) pattern in the affected CHECKs, or
  explicitly documenting that DB-level normalization only covers plain spaces
  and full whitespace normalization is an application-layer responsibility.

  2. lower() is ASCII-only case folding, so non-ASCII company/location names 
  bypass normalized uniqueness. Confirmed empirically: 'Café Corp' and 'CAFÉ 
  CORP' are not treated as duplicates by the idx_company_name_normalized index.
  Architecture requires uniqueness "using normalized comparison that ignores
  letter case" with no ASCII carve-out. This is a real gap for any accented
  company/location name and isn't documented anywhere as a known limitation.
  Recommend at minimum recording this as a known Phase 1 limitation in the ADR
  (loading SQLite's ICU extension is likely disproportionate for this phase).

  3. The AFTER UPDATE triggers bump last_updated_at even on no-op updates.
  Confirmed empirically: updating a company's name to its existing value still
  changes last_updated_at. This contradicts the architecture's explicit
  statement that "reusing an unchanged reference record does not constitute a
  modification to that record." The schema alone can't guarantee this invariant
  — future CRUD code will need to avoid issuing no-op UPDATEs (e.g., diff before
  writing). Worth adding as a forward-looking note in the ADR's "Consequences"
  section; it's currently undocumented.

  Low

  4. display_order INTEGER NOT NULL UNIQUE on STATUS is stricter than 
  architecture literally requires (it only says display_order "controls logical
  presentation order," not that it must be unique). Confirmed enforced via test.
  Reasonable choice, but it's an inferred decision not mentioned in the ADR
  alongside the other documented inferences.

  5. The effective_at format CHECK ends in an unconstrained GLOB wildcard (*),
  so a value like '2026-09-20T09:00:00GARBAGE' passes the database-level format
  check (confirmed empirically). The ADR already defers full validation to the
  application layer, so this isn't wrong, but the check is looser than it may
  appear — a tighter pattern (requiring . + 3 digits + Z) would track the
  documented convention more closely while still stopping short of full
  validation.

  6. Trigger non-recursion depends on SQLite's recursive_triggers pragma 
  remaining at its default OFF, which connect() never sets explicitly.
  Confirmed: enabling it causes OperationalError: too many levels of trigger 
  recursion on any UPDATE. Nothing in this codebase turns it on today, but the
  safety is an implicit, undocumented dependency on a connection default rather
  than something the code defends itself against.

  7. STRICT tables require SQLite ≥ 3.37; nothing pins or checks this as a 
  minimum requirement outside the ADR's observational note (current environment:
  3.46.1). Running against an older bundled SQLite would fail flask init-db
  with a bare syntax error, without a diagnostic pointing at the real cause.

  Confirmed correct (no issues)

  - All six tables and all six documented relationships present with correct
  nullability/cardinality.
  - PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON applied uniformly through the single connect()
  chokepoint used by get_db(), the CLI command, and tests — confirmed via test
  and manual check.
  - close_db via teardown_appcontext correctly closes the connection on
  app-context exit — confirmed empirically (Cannot operate on a closed database
  after context pop), no leak.
  - Compensation min ≤ max and compensation_basis-required-when-present CHECK
  logic verified correct for all presence combinations.
  - STRICT-table typing genuinely rejects a non-numeric compensation value
  (IntegrityError), satisfying "not relying on a numeric-looking declaration
  alone."
  - Status seed values, display order (1–8), and terminal-state assignment match
  architecture's listed values; seeding is idempotent (INSERT OR IGNORE against
  UNIQUE(name)) — confirmed no duplication on repeated init_db().
  - Initialization is non-destructive and repeatable — confirmed a pre-existing
  row survives a second init_db() call and tables are never dropped (CREATE 
  TABLE IF NOT EXISTS).
  - Tests are fully isolated (all via tmp_path, never touching the default
  instance-path DB) and meaningfully exercise the documented constraints rather
  than superficial existence checks.
  - No SQL is built from untrusted input anywhere in this slice (schema.sql is
  static DDL; db.py has no dynamic query construction); no SQL-injection surface
  exists yet.
  - No CRUD routes, workflows, or functionality outside the declared scope;
  pyproject.toml diff is empty — no new dependencies, no ORM introduced.
  - ADR is consistent with the implementation for everything it documents; the
  gaps above are omissions, not contradictions.

  Recommendation

  Nothing here blocks a commit of this foundational slice — the gaps are all
  edge cases (non-ASCII names, tab-only whitespace, no-op updates) that don't
  affect the documented happy-path behavior or the six-table structure. If
  tightening before commit, I'd prioritize #1 and #2 (both are concrete,
  empirically-confirmed correctness gaps against explicit architecture language)
  and add #3 as an ADR note so it isn't silently rediscovered when CRUD code is
  written next.

● Summary of changes

  src/job_hub/schema.sql
  - Finding 1 (whitespace validation): every blank-rejection CHECK
  (company.name, source.name, status.name, application.job_title) and every
  normalized-uniqueness index expression (company, source, location) now trims
  char(32)||char(9)||char(13)||char(10) (space, tab, CR, LF) instead of relying
  on SQLite's default trim(), which only strips plain spaces. The LOCATION "at
  least one real component" CHECK uses the same character set. A header comment
  documents the convention and points to the ADR.
  - Finding 3 (no-op updates): all six AFTER UPDATE triggers gained a WHEN
  clause comparing every non-metadata column between OLD and NEW via IS NOT
  (correct for nullable columns like hq_location_id). last_updated_at now only
  advances when a real value actually changed.
  - Finding 2 required no schema change (see below).

  docs/decisions/0001-phase-1-sqlite-persistence-foundation.md
  - Added a "no-op update" paragraph under the timestamp section explaining the
  WHEN-guarded triggers.
  - Added a new "Insignificant whitespace convention" subsection defining
  space/tab/CR/LF and noting it's applied consistently to both blank checks and
  uniqueness indexes.
  - Added a new "Known limitation: non-ASCII case folding" subsection explicitly
  documenting that SQLite's lower() is ASCII-only, giving a concrete example,
  and recording the decision not to introduce ICU/custom collation for Phase 1
  (Finding 2 — documentation-only per your instruction, no code change).
  - Added two "Consequences" bullets: the accepted non-ASCII limitation, and a
  maintenance note that future columns must be added to the relevant trigger's
  WHEN clause.

  tests/test_db.py
  - Added WHITESPACE_ONLY_VALUES = [" ", "\t", "\r", "\n", " \t\r\n "].
  - Replaced the old single-case test_company_blank_name_is_rejected with

  - A LocationInput dataclass (city/state_province/country) reused for both job
  location and company headquarters.
  - A ValidationError exception for Python-level validation failures (required
  fields, documented enum values), kept distinct from sqlite3.IntegrityError
  (DB-constraint failures) so a future route can handle each differently.
  - Reference resolution (company, source, location) looks up existing rows
  using the same SQL normalization expression already encoded in the schema's
  unique indexes (lower(trim(x, char(32)||char(9)||char(13)||char(10)))), rather
  than reimplementing normalization in Python — this guarantees the lookup can
  never drift from the DB's own uniqueness rule. Python does trim text before
  storage (FR-011), using the identical " \t\r\n" character set the ADR already
  defines, so Python and SQL agree on "insignificant whitespace."
  - Company resolution looks up by normalized name first; only if no match
  exists does it resolve/create an optional headquarters location and insert the
  new company. This avoids creating an orphaned LOCATION row for an HQ that
  would be discarded anyway when an existing company is reused (architecture:
  "selecting an existing company uses its existing headquarters location").
  - The initial STATUS row is looked up by name (default "APPLIED"), never a
  hardcoded ID.
  - Initial effective date/time defaults follow FR-001 literally: when status is
  APPLIED and application_date equals today (UTC), effective timestamp
  auto-defaults to "now" (injectable via a now parameter for deterministic
  tests, per the architecture's testability guidance). In every other case
  (non-APPLIED status, or a non-today application_date), an explicit effective
  timestamp is required — if missing, that's a validation failure, not a silent
  default. Effective timestamps in the future are also rejected (FR-011's
  future-timestamp rule, which nothing else enforces since the DB only checks
  structural format).
  - Everything runs on one connection with one commit at the end; any exception
  triggers connection.rollback() and re-raises, satisfying the "no partial data"
  requirement.
  - Per "don't duplicate every DB rule in Python," I deliberately do not
  re-validate compensation min≤max or compensation-basis-required-when-present
  in Python — those stay DB-CHECK-only, giving a genuine DB-constraint-failure
  path to test.

  Ambiguity flagged before implementing: the task's phrasing groups source with
  location as "supplied when optional" ("Resolve or create SOURCE ... when a 
  source is supplied", "optional source/location behavior as documented"). But
  mvp-requirements.md FR-001 explicitly states "Source - Required", and
  architecture.md's APPLICATION.source_id is "Required foreign key to SOURCE" —
  only job_location_id is documented as optional. I'm implementing source as
  required (matching the explicit requirements/architecture over the looser task
  phrasing) and job_location as the only genuinely optional reference
  resolution, and I'm adding tests that pin down both behaviors explicitly so
  this decision is visible rather than silent.

  Proceeding with implementation.

● Summary

  Files created:
  - src/job_hub/applications.py — create_application() business/persistence
  function plus LocationInput, CreateApplicationResult, and ValidationError.
  - tests/test_applications.py — 17 focused tests.

  No existing files were modified; nothing committed.

  Behavior implemented:
  - Validates required fields (company name, job title, application date, source
  name — all non-blank after trimming) and documented enumerated values
  (work_arrangement, employment_type, compensation_basis), raising
  ValidationError before any database writes occur.
  - Resolves-or-creates COMPANY, SOURCE, and LOCATION (job location and, only
  for a brand-new company, headquarters) using the exact SQL normalization
  expression already encoded in the schema's unique indexes — so lookups can't
  drift from the DB's own uniqueness rule. An existing company's headquarters is
  never touched or overwritten, and no orphan LOCATION row is created for an HQ
  input that ends up unused (fixed during testing — see below).
  - Looks up the initial STATUS row by name (default APPLIED) rather than a
  hardcoded ID; unknown names raise ValidationError.
  - Implements FR-001's initial-effective-timestamp defaulting literally:
  auto-defaults to "now" only when status is APPLIED and application_date is
  today (UTC, via an injectable now for deterministic tests); every other case
  requires an explicit effective timestamp. Future timestamps are rejected.
  - Runs reference resolution, APPLICATION insert, and
  APPLICATION_STATUS_HISTORY insert as one transaction on the caller's
  connection, committing once at the end; any exception triggers
  connection.rollback() and re-raises.
  - Deliberately leaves compensation-range and compensation-basis-required
  checks to the existing DB CHECK constraints rather than duplicating them in
  Python.
  - Returns a CreateApplicationResult with the new application ID plus resolved
  company/source/location/status/history IDs.

  Ambiguity resolved (not silently invented): the task prompt implied source
  might be optional like location, but mvp-requirements.md FR-001 and
  architecture.md's APPLICATION.source_id both explicitly mark source as
  required. Implemented accordingly — job_location is the only optional
  reference resolution — and added
  test_source_is_required/test_job_location_is_optional to make the decision
  explicit and verified.

  Bug caught during implementation: my first draft eagerly resolved/created the
  company's HQ location before checking whether the company already existed
  (Python evaluates call arguments before the call), which would have created an
  orphan LOCATION row whenever an existing company's HQ input didn't match. The
  test_existing_company_headquarters_is_not_overwritten test caught this; fixed
  by moving HQ-location resolution inside _resolve_or_create_company, only
  reached on the "company not found" branch.

  Tests added (17): successful creation; initial status + history creation;
  default-effective-at-when-today; explicit retrospective status/effective-at;
  missing-required-effective-at validation; future-effective-at validation;
  unknown-status validation; company/source/location reuse across
  case/whitespace variants; new-reference-record creation; new-company-HQ
  creation and linkage; existing-company-HQ preservation (with orphan-location
  check); job-location-optional; source-required; blank-job-title validation
  (asserting zero writes); invalid-enum validation (asserting zero writes); DB
  constraint failure (compensation min>max); full transaction rollback on a
  later DB failure (asserting no company/source/application/history rows

● Review Summary

  Reviewed src/job_hub/applications.py and tests/test_applications.py against
  the doc set, re-read the code fresh, and ran targeted empirical checks (not
  just the existing test suite) to probe edge cases the tests don't cover. All
  56 existing tests still pass; pyproject.toml is unchanged (no new
  dependencies). Found one real, empirically-confirmed defect.

  Medium

  1. A timezone-naive now override crashes with a raw TypeError instead of a 
  clean ValidationError. Confirmed empirically:

  create_application(conn, ..., now=datetime(2026, 9, 20, 15, 0, 0))  # no 
  tzinfo
  # TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes

  _resolve_initial_effective_at defensively normalizes effective_at's tzinfo
  before comparing it to now, but never applies the same normalization to now
  itself — so a naive now blows up in the final future-timestamp comparison.
  This is exactly the kind of mistake a future test author (or a route calling
  something datetime.utcnow()-shaped) could make, and it directly undermines the
  now-injection mechanism that architecture.md explicitly calls for as the
  testability pattern for "a small, controllable time boundary." Recommend
  normalizing now's tzinfo once, in create_application, before it's used
  anywhere.

  Low

  2. Inconsistent validation ordering. Required-field/enum checks run before the
  try block (confirmed: zero writes on failure), but unknown-status-name and
  missing/future-effective-at checks run inside the try, relying on
  connection.rollback() being a harmless no-op when nothing's been written
  (confirmed empirically — it is). Functionally fine, but moving those two
  checks before the try would make "validate everything, then write everything"
  uniform.

  3. Only one of the two compensation CHECK constraints is exercised through 
  this layer (min > max); "compensation basis required when compensation
  present" isn't separately tested via create_application (though it's already
  covered directly against the schema in test_db.py, and the code path handling
  both is identical). Minor coverage gap, not a functional one.

  4. The nested .format() SQL-building in _resolve_or_create_location
  (_NORMALIZE_SQL.format(expr="coalesce({0}, '')"), then
  .format('city')/.format('?')) is correct and safe — verified only fixed
  column-name/placeholder literals ever pass through .format(); real values are
  always bound parameters, so there's no injection risk — but it's denser than
  the "straightforward" bar elsewhere in the codebase.

  5. create_application implicitly assumes it owns the connection's entire 
  transaction (unconditional commit/rollback at the end). This matches
  architecture's framing of application creation as one atomic operation, but
  it's a contract worth a one-line note for whoever wires up the future Flask
  route: never call this mid-way through other unrelated uncommitted work on the
  same connection.

  Confirmed correct (no issues)

  - Field handling (required vs. optional, defaults) matches FR-001 exactly,
  including the effective-date/time defaulting rule transcribed literally
  (auto-default only when status is APPLIED and application_date is today;
  explicit value required otherwise; future timestamps rejected).
  - Company/source/location reuse queries use the identical SQL normalization
  expression as the schema's own unique indexes (verified side-by-side against
  schema.sql), so lookups can't drift from the DB's uniqueness rule.
  - HQ location is only resolved/created for a genuinely new company — confirmed
  no orphan LOCATION row and no change to an existing company's hq_location_id
  or last_updated_at on reuse.
  - Reference-data reuse never issues an UPDATE, so the ADR's no-op-update
  invariant is trivially satisfied here — confirmed empirically (created_at == 
  last_updated_at after reuse).
  - Transaction rollback correctly undoes company/source/application/history
  writes together on a later failure (test + manual verification of sqlite3's
  implicit-transaction semantics).
  - Duplicate-application handling is correctly absent — two applications with
  identical company+job title succeed, matching architecture's explicit "no
  database uniqueness restriction" on that combination (confirmed empirically).
  - Compensation-range/basis rules are correctly left to DB CHECK constraints
  rather than duplicated in Python.
  - All SQL is parameterized; string-built fragments are only fixed column
  names/placeholders, never user data.
  - No ORM, framework, or new dependency introduced.
  - Tests are isolated (fresh temp DB per test) and cover all eight required
  categories.

  Recommendation

  Fix #1 before commit — it's a real, reproducible crash in the explicit
  testability mechanism the architecture asked for, and cheap to fix (normalize
  now's tzinfo once at the top of create_application). #2–#5 are minor and can
  reasonably be deferred or bundled into a later cleanup pass.

● Summary

  Root fix — src/job_hub/__init__.py: create_app() now calls
  db.init_db(db.get_db()) unconditionally inside an app context, right after
  db.init_app(app). This is safe on every startup because init_db is fully
  idempotent (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + INSERT OR IGNORE seeding) — it never
  drops tables, never duplicates seed rows, and never touches existing data, so
  "ordinary startup shall not reset existing data" still holds. The flask 
  init-db CLI command still exists for manual/scripted use, but is no longer
  required for the app to work.

  Test-isolation fix — this is what makes the auto-init safe: since create_app()
  now always touches its configured DATABASE, any test calling it without an
  override would have started touching the real default
  instance/job_hub.sqlite3. Fixed by giving every test that builds a real app an
  isolated DATABASE (a tmp_path file), matching the pattern already used
  elsewhere:
  - tests/test_factory.py — added an _isolated_config(tmp_path) helper; both
  existing tests now use it.
  - tests/test_home_route.py — the client fixture now builds create_app() with a
  tmp_path-based TestConfig instead of the bare default.
  - tests/test_application_routes.py — simplified: its app fixture no longer
  needs the manual db.init_db(db.get_db()) call, since create_app() now does it
  automatically.

  Tests added (2, in test_factory.py):
  test_create_app_automatically_initializes_database_schema (fresh create_app(),
  no manual init call, queries status and gets the 8 seeded rows) and
  test_create_app_initialization_is_idempotent_across_repeated_calls (calls
  create_app() twice on the same DB path, confirms seed data isn't duplicated).

  Documentation: updated
  docs/decisions/0001-phase-1-sqlite-persistence-foundation.md's "Initialization
  trigger point" section (and its Consequences bullet) to record the revision —
  the original explicit-only decision was marked provisional pending CRUD
  routes; this closes that loop with the actual reasoning, not just a silent
  change.

  Manual verification (not just the test suite): deleted any local instance/
  directory, started the real dev server with no prior flask init-db, and
  confirmed GET / → 200, GET /applications/new → 200 with the status dropdown
  populated, and POST /applications/new → 302 (application created) — proving a
  genuinely fresh checkout no longer 500s. Cleaned up the scratch database
  afterward.

  Test result: pytest -v → 69 passed, 0 failed (0.92s).

  Nothing committed; working tree only contains the intended changes (verified
  via git status).

● Review Summary

  Reviewed the diff for the Create Application UI slice
  (src/job_hub/__init__.py, applications.py's enum-tuple change, routes.py,
  templates/base.html, templates/applications/new.html, static/css/style.css,
  the ADR, and the three touched/added test files) against the doc set, and ran
  targeted empirical checks beyond the existing test suite (XSS escaping,
  non-finite compensation values, end-to-end transaction rollback through the
  HTTP layer, and a full-suite grep for test isolation). All 69 existing tests
  still pass. No files were modified.

  Medium

  1. Compensation parsing accepts non-finite values (nan, inf) and they reach 
  the database. _parse_compensation in routes.py calls bare float(value), which
  happily parses "nan"/"inf"/"infinity". Confirmed end-to-end through the real
  HTTP route:
  - compensation_max=inf (with a finite compensation_min) is silently accepted
  (302 success) and persisted verbatim — SELECT compensation_max FROM 
  application returns inf. SQLite STRICT REAL columns don't reject IEEE-754
  infinity, and neither the DB CHECK constraints nor applications.py validate
  finiteness.
  - compensation_min=nan is silently coerced to NULL by the SQLite driver on
  storage — the request succeeds (302), the user gets no error, and their
  entered value simply vanishes without a trace.

  A real browser's native <input type="number"> blocks typing these strings, so
  this needs a non-browser client or a modified request — but it's fully
  reachable through the documented workflow, and architecture.md explicitly
  anticipates future "filtering, sorting, or analysis" of compensation data,
  which an inf row would break. Recommend rejecting non-finite values in
  _parse_compensation (e.g. math.isfinite) before they reach the service.

  2. No per-field error marking or ARIA live-region wiring. The single
  #form-error paragraph does include the failing field's name as text (e.g.
  "job_title: is required"), which minimally satisfies FR-011's "clear
  indication of the invalid field or condition," but: the specific
  <input>/<select> that failed isn't marked in any way (no aria-invalid, no
  adjacent per-field message, no visual highlight), and neither #form-error nor
  #flash-messages carries role="alert"/role="status"/aria-live — confirmed via
  grep, zero role=/aria- attributes exist anywhere in either template. A
  screen-reader user wouldn't be automatically notified of a validation failure
  or a successful save. Worth closing now, before it becomes the established
  pattern for future forms.

  Low

  3. Required fields are indicated only via the native HTML required attribute —
  no visible in-page text/asterisk marks them, a softer reading of NFR-001's
  "forms shall identify required information."

  4. When a submitted company_hq_location doesn't apply because the company
  already exists (correct, documented behavior per architecture.md), the UI
  gives no feedback that the entered headquarters data was discarded. Not a
  defect — there's no detail view yet to surface the discrepancy — but worth a
  note for when list/detail work lands.

  5. A few edge cases are correct (verified manually in this review) but not
  asserted by an automated test at the route layer specifically: whitespace-only
  (not just empty-string) required-field submission, a tampered
  initial_status_name not present in the seeded dropdown, and full transaction
  rollback through the HTTP stack (service-layer rollback is already tested in
  test_applications.py, but not re-asserted at the route level).

  Confirmed correct — no issues found

  - FR-001 field coverage is complete on the form.
  - Reflected form values are safely Jinja-autoescaped — verified empirically
  with both an attribute-breakout payload (" onmouseover="..) and a
  <textarea>-breakout payload (</textarea><script>...); neither escaped its
  context.
  - Full transaction rollback (no orphan company/source/application rows)
  verified end-to-end through the actual HTTP route, not just the service layer.
  - Automatic schema initialization is idempotent, and every create_app() call
  across the entire test suite supplies an isolated DATABASE path (confirmed by
  grep) — no test touches the real default instance-path database.
  - No SQL injection surface — the route's only literal SQL (_status_options) is
  a static string; everything else flows through the already-parameterized
  create_application().
  - No CSRF protection, consistent with the already-documented, reasonable Phase
  1 scope decision (no auth/multi-user session model).
  - No accidental scope creep — the diff is confined to the create-application
  route/template/nav/CSS, the enum-tuple refactor that serves it, and the
  separately-requested auto-init change.
  - ADR 0001's revised "Initialization trigger point" section accurately
  describes the actual code change.
  - Stable, meaningful, non-duplicated id/name selectors throughout, with
  error-message field names matching real form field names.

  Recommendation

  Fix #1 before commit — it's a reproducible data-integrity gap reachable
  through the documented workflow, cheap to close (one finiteness check), and
  exactly the kind of thing that's much harder to clean up once real data exists
  in the database. #2 is worth addressing now given how easily the pattern will
  propagate to future forms, but is not a blocking correctness issue. #3–#5 are
  minor and can reasonably be deferred.

      334 +        c.name AS company_name,                               
      335 +        a.job_title,                                          
      336 +        l.city AS job_location_city,                          
      337 +        l.state_province AS job_location_state_province,      
      338 +        l.country AS job_location_country,                    
      339 +        a.work_arrangement,                                   
      340 +        a.application_date,                                   
      341 +        s.name AS source_name,                                
      342 +        st.name AS status_name                                
      343 +    FROM application a                                        
      344 +    JOIN company c ON c.company_id = a.company_id             
      345 +    JOIN source s ON s.source_id = a.source_id                
      346 +    LEFT JOIN location l ON l.location_id = a.job_location_id 
      347 +    JOIN current_status cs ON cs.application_id = a.applicatio
          +n_id                                                          
      348 +    JOIN status st ON st.status_id = cs.status_id             
      349 +    WHERE a.archived_at IS NULL                               
      350 +    ORDER BY {order_by}                                       
      351 +    LIMIT ? OFFSET ?                                          
      352 +"""                                                           
      353 +                                                              
      354 +                                                              
      355 +def list_applications(                                        
      356 +    connection,                                               
      357 +    *,                                                        
      358 +    sort=LIST_DEFAULT_SORT,                                   
      359 +    direction=LIST_DEFAULT_DIRECTION,                         
      360 +    page=1,                                                   
      361 +) -> ApplicationListPage:                                     
      362 +    if sort not in LIST_SORT_COLUMNS:                         
      363 +        sort = LIST_DEFAULT_SORT                              
      364 +    if direction not in ("asc", "desc"):                      
      365 +        direction = LIST_DEFAULT_DIRECTION                    
      366 +    if not isinstance(page, int) or page < 1:                 
      367 +        page = 1                                              
      368 +                                                              
      369 +    total_count = connection.execute(                         
      370 +        "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM application WHERE archived_
          +at IS NULL"                                                   
      371 +    ).fetchone()["n"]                                         
      372 +                                                              
      373 +    page_size = LIST_PAGE_SIZE                                
      374 +    total_pages = max(1, -(-total_count // page_size))        
      375 +    if page > total_pages:                                    
      376 +        page = total_pages                                    
      377 +    offset = (page - 1) * page_size                           
      378 +                                                              
      379 +    sql_direction = "ASC" if direction == "asc" else "DESC"   
      380 +    order_terms = [f"{column} {sql_direction}" for column in L
          +IST_SORT_COLUMNS[sort]]                                       
      381 +    order_terms.append(f"a.application_id {sql_direction}")   
      382 +    order_by = ", ".join(order_terms)                         
      383 +                                                              
      384 +    rows = connection.execute(                                
      385 +        _LIST_QUERY.format(order_by=order_by), (page_size, off
          +set)                                                          
      386 +    ).fetchall()                                              
      387 +                                                              
      388 +    items = [                                                 
      389 +        ApplicationListItem(                                  
      390 +            application_id=row["application_id"],             
      391 +            company_name=row["company_name"],                 
      392 +            job_title=row["job_title"],                       
      393 +            job_location_city=row["job_location_city"],       
      394 +            job_location_state_province=row["job_location_stat
          +e_province"],                                                 
      395 +            job_location_country=row["job_location_country"], 
      396 +            work_arrangement=row["work_arrangement"],         
      397 +            application_date=row["application_date"],         
      398 +            source_name=row["source_name"],                   
      399 +            status_name=row["status_name"],                   
      400 +        )                                                     
      401 +        for row in rows                                       
      402 +    ]                                                         
      403 +                                                              
      404 +    return ApplicationListPage(                               
      405 +        items=items,                                          
      406 +        sort=sort,                                            
      407 +        direction=direction,                                  
      408 +        page=page,                                            
      409 +        page_size=page_size,                                  
      410 +        total_count=total_count,                              
      411 +    )

● Good — confirms the Create Application UI slice was committed between turns,
  and today's diff is cleanly scoped to just the List slice. All 97 tests pass,

  Summary

  Files created:
  - src/job_hub/templates/applications/list.html — the applications table (or
  empty-state message), sortable column headers, pagination controls.
  - tests/test_application_list.py — 12 service-level tests for
  list_applications().
  - tests/test_application_list_routes.py — 12 route/template-level tests.

  Files modified:
  - src/job_hub/applications.py — added list_applications(),
  ApplicationListItem/ApplicationListPage dataclasses, and the sort-column
  whitelist. One query derives each application's current status via
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY effective_at DESC)
  (matching architecture.md's mandated derivation) and joins
  company/source/location/status in a single statement; a second, constant-cost
  COUNT(*) query supports pagination math. Verified via EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN that
  all joins resolve through indexed/PK lookups — no N+1.
  - src/job_hub/routes.py — added GET /applications; parses sort/dir/page query
  params (invalid values silently fall back to defaults rather than raising,
  since these are URL parameters, not submitted form data). Also changed the
  create-application success redirect from the home page to the new list page
  (see note below).
  - src/job_hub/templates/base.html — added an "Applications" nav link.
  - src/job_hub/static/css/style.css — minimal table/pagination/empty-state
  styling.

  Behavior implemented (FR-003): all seven documented columns (Company, Job
  title, Job location, Work arrangement, Application date, Current status,
  Source) displayed by name/value, never raw IDs; default sort is application
  date descending; all seven columns are click-sortable with
  ascending/descending toggle (aria-sort on the active <th>); pagination at the
  documented page size of 25, with Previous/Next controls that are absent (not
  just disabled) when everything fits on one page; an explicit empty-state
  message (#applications-empty-state) instead of an empty/broken table when no
  applications exist.

  Verified via tests + manual checks: current status correctly reflects the
  latest effective_at history row, not the initial status; missing optional job
  location renders as "—", not blank or broken; company name is HTML-escaped in
  the list (tested with a <script> payload); default ordering and column sorting
  behave correctly; pagination math (25/page, boundary clamping) is correct;
  archived applications (archived_at set) are excluded from the list even though
  no route sets that column yet.

  Test result: pytest -v → 97 passed, 0 failed (1.70s) — all 73 pre-existing
  tests remain green.

  Ambiguities identified (not silently decided)

  1. Slice scope. The task's exclusion list
  (detail/edit/status-change/archive/reference-data/Selenium) notably did not
  mention sort/filter/pagination, unlike every prior slice in this session. I
  interpreted "the application list" as FR-003 in full (list + default/column
  sorting + pagination), since FR-003's sort/paginate requirements are explicit
  "shall" statements, not ambiguous product behavior, and FR-004 (Search and
  Filter) is a separately-named requirement I left out — partly because it's
  genuinely a different feature, and partly because its record-state
  (Active/Archived/All) filtering is meaningless without archive/restore, which
  is explicitly excluded here. Flagging this scope call for confirmation rather
  than assuming it's correct.
  2. "Job location" sort key. FR-003 doesn't define what a compound field sorts
  by. I sort by (city, state_province, country) in that order — a reasonable but
  undocumented choice.
  3. "Current status" sort key. I sort by STATUS.display_order (the field
  architecture.md describes as "logical presentation order") rather than
  alphabetically by status name, since alphabetical order would scatter
  lifecycle-adjacent statuses randomly. Not explicitly specified by FR-003.
  4. Job location display format ("City, State, Province" comma-joined, skipping
  blank components) and the "—" placeholder for missing optional values are
  formatting choices with no documented precedent (no detail view exists yet to
  match against).

  Intentionally deferred

  - Detail view, editing, status changes, archive/restore, reference-data
  management, Selenium — per explicit exclusion.
  - FR-004 search/filter and record-state (Active/Archived/All) filtering — see
  ambiguity #1.
  - "Selecting an application" (FR-003's link to the detail view) is not
  implemented — rows are plain table data, since the detail view they'd link to
  doesn't exist yet. This is a direct, unavoidable consequence of the
  detail-view exclusion, not a gap.

  One behavior change worth flagging explicitly

  The create-application form's post-success redirect now points to
  /applications instead of / (home), since a meaningful destination now exists.
  This modifies behavior from the already-committed Create Application slice
  rather than being purely additive; low-risk (confirmed via the existing,
  unmodified test_post_valid_application_creates_and_redirects test still
  passing, since it only checks the flash message renders after following the
  redirect, not the specific URL) but noting it since it wasn't explicitly
  requested.

  correction; current status derived from the already-fetched status history
  (last entry, guaranteed unique) rather than a redundant query; job location
  and company HQ fetched via two independent LOCATION joins so they stay
  distinct even when identical (tested); current status marked both visually and
  via aria-current="true"; compensation fields shown individually only when

  filter by archived_at (detail-by-ID should survive archiving, per FR-009's
  preservation guarantee — currently moot but recorded); closing the FR-003 gap

  404 handling as necessary-but-unspecified basic behavior.

  Bug caught during self-review: job_url (never format-validated, by earlier
  deliberate design) was rendered directly into href, so a stored
  javascript:alert(...) value became an executable link — a real stored-XSS
  vector. Fixed by only rendering job_url as a clickable <a> for http/https
  schemes; anything else displays as inert escaped text. Added regression tests
  at both layers. Also independently verified (beyond the automated tests):
  non-integer/nonexistent IDs 404 cleanly, and reflected values are correctly
  escaped in the <title> tag, not just the body.

● Let me empirically verify a few things: compensation float display formatting,
  and integer-converter edge cases (negative/oversized IDs).

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● Review Summary

  Reviewed the Application Detail implementation fresh against FR-005,
  architecture.md, development-process.md, test-strategy.md, and ADR 0001. All
  119 existing tests still pass. Ran targeted empirical checks beyond the
  existing test suite (compensation display formatting, and application-ID edge
  cases: negative, zero, oversized). No files were modified.

  Medium

  1. An oversized application_id crashes with an unhandled OverflowError, not a 
  clean 404. Confirmed reproducible:
  GET /applications/99999999999999999999999999999999
  → 500 Internal Server Error
  OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to SQLite INTEGER
  Flask's <int:...> converter has no upper bound (its regex is just \d+), so any
  sufficiently large digit string in the path reaches get_application_detail()
  and blows up inside the sqlite3 driver before the "no such row → 404" path is
  ever reached. Negative IDs and zero both correctly 404 (confirmed), so this is
  specific to the overflow case. This is a real, trivially reachable,
  unauthenticated crash — low real-world impact for a local single-user Phase 1
  app, but exactly the kind of unhandled exception that should degrade to a 404
  rather than leak a stack trace (relevant given how carefully the DEBUG flag
  was handled earlier in this project). Recommend catching OverflowError (or
  bounding the accepted ID range) before it reaches the query.

  2. Compensation values display with a spurious trailing .0. Confirmed
  empirically: entering compensation_min=100000 renders as 100000.0 in the
  detail page, because the value round-trips through a STRICT REAL column as a
  Python float and Jinja's default {{ }} calls str() on it. Not a functional
  bug, but a real, user-visible quality gap on a field FR-005 explicitly calls
  out ("Minimum and maximum compensation when available") — a personal
  compensation-tracking field showing "100000.0" reads as
  unpolished/unintentional. Recommend formatting (e.g., strip a trailing .0 for
  whole values, or a light numeric formatter) before display.

  Low

  3. "Back to Applications" always returns to the list's default view,
  discarding any sort column/direction/page the user was previously on. Not
  required by any FR, but a foreseeable rough edge — a user three pages deep in
  a sorted list who opens a detail page and clicks back lands back on page 1,
  default sort.

  4. Inconsistent "optional field absent" presentation within the same 
  Application section. work_arrangement/employment_type always render a
  <dt>/<dd> pair with a "—" placeholder;
  compensation_min/compensation_max/compensation_basis are omitted entirely (no
  <dt> at all) when absent. Not wrong — FR-005's "when available" phrasing
  arguably supports the compensation approach more literally — but it's an
  internal inconsistency within one section that a careful reader will notice.

  5. The four detail <section> elements have no accessible name
  (aria-labelledby/aria-label), so none are exposed as navigable landmark
  regions to assistive technology, despite each having a visible <h3>. The page
  remains fully readable via heading-based navigation, so this is an enhancement
  rather than a blocking failure — but "accessibility" was an explicit review
  focus, so worth naming: pointing each <section aria-labelledby="..."> at its
  heading id would close this cheaply.

  6. Status-history effective_at values render as raw ISO-8601-with-milliseconds
  strings (2026-09-20T15:00:00.000Z) rather than a human-readable format.
  Consistent with the list view's existing raw-date precedent (not a new
  inconsistency introduced here), just a shared minor polish opportunity.

  Confirmed correct — no issues found

  - All four FR-005 sections present with exactly the documented fields.
  - Company headquarters and job location remain genuinely distinct even when
  they resolve to the same normalized LOCATION row (two independent
  joins/aliases) — confirmed by test and by re-reading the query.
  - Current-status derivation reuses the already-fetched, ascending-ordered
  history rather than a redundant query, and correctly reflects the latest
  effective_at regardless of insertion order — matches architecture.md's "same
  derivation" rule.
  - No optional field can crash the view or render a misleading value —
  confirmed for every optional field.
  - Job-URL handling is a correctly-designed allowlist (http/https only), not a
  narrow javascript:-only patch — it also blocks data:, vbscript:, etc. by
  construction; Jinja's autoescaping independently closes attribute-breakout
  regardless of scheme.
  - Negative and zero application IDs correctly 404.
  - Reflected values (notes, job title, company name) are correctly escaped,
  including inside <title>.
  - List↔detail navigation both present and working.
  - No SQL injection surface — both queries are static, parameterized only by
  application_id.
  - No unintended scope expansion — diff is confined to the detail view, the
  previously-flagged FR-003 list-link completion, and the job-URL security fix,
  all documented in the journal.
  - No N+1 concern — two queries total per detail view (not list-scale).

  Recommendation

  Fix #1 and #2 before commit — both are concrete, reproducible, and cheap to
  address (a bounds/exception check and a small display-formatting tweak). #3–#6
  are reasonable to defer or bundle into a later polish pass; none block
  committing this slice.

  - Exactly 2**63 - 1 (SQLite's max, a valid-but-nonexistent ID) → 404, no
  crash.
  - 2**63 (one past the boundary, triggers the OverflowError) → 404, cleanly
  caught.

  unaffected — the except OverflowError is narrowly scoped and never engages for

  404 path.

  written test cases:
  - _format_number(0.0) → "0" (not swallowed by a None/falsy-style check —

  uses is not none, so a genuine $0 compensation value correctly renders its row
  rather than being treated as absent).

  - End-to-end: a real $0/$0 compensation submission renders

● Next Slice: FR-006 — Edit an Application

  Requirement

  FR-006 — Edit an Application (docs/mvp-requirements.md)

  ▎ The system shall allow information associated with an existing application 
  ▎ to be edited.

  Acceptance criteria, as documented:

  - Editable fields: Company, Job title, Application date, Job location, Company
  headquarters location, Job description, Job URL, External job/requisition ID,
  Source, Work arrangement, Employment type, Minimum compensation, Maximum
  compensation, Compensation basis, Notes.
  - The same field validation rules that apply when recording an application
  apply when editing.
  - Editing shall not modify or replace application status history.
  - Application status shall not be changed through the general edit operation
  (that's FR-007, a separate requirement).
  - When company headquarters information is edited, the change applies to the
  COMPANY record and may therefore affect other applications associated with the
  same company.
  - The system shall require confirmation before applying a company-level change
  that affects information shared by multiple applications.
  - Saving updates last_updated_at while preserving the original created_at.
  - The user shall be able to cancel an edit without changing persisted data.

  Supporting architecture.md text: "Selecting an existing company uses its
  existing headquarters location. Changing an application's company shall
  therefore display the selected company's headquarters rather than carry over
  the previous company's headquarters," and "Headquarters changes modify shared
  company data. When a company-level change affects information shared by
  multiple applications, the user must confirm it before persistence, as
  specified by FR-006." Transaction Boundaries: editing "follows the same
  [atomicity] principle when it creates reference data or applies a confirmed
  shared company change."

  Why this is the appropriate next slice

  FR-005 (just completed) is the pivot: it's the page from which an "Edit"
  action would launch, and nothing about company/status editing was buildable
  before a record could be viewed. Among the remaining unimplemented
  requirements (FR-002, FR-004, FR-006–FR-009), FR-006 is the one FR-005 most
  directly unlocks, and it continues the natural CRUD build order this project
  has followed so far: Create (FR-001) → List (FR-003) → Detail (FR-005) → Edit 
  (FR-006).

  It also reuses the most existing infrastructure of any candidate:
  applications.py's private validation helpers (_require_text, _require_enum,
  _trim) and resolve-or-create logic (_resolve_or_create_company,
  _resolve_or_create_source, _resolve_or_create_location) were all built for
  create_application and are directly applicable to an edit path with no
  persistence-layer changes needed — the schema's last_updated_at triggers
  already only advance on a genuine value change (built and tested in the
  persistence-foundation slice specifically to satisfy this FR-006 requirement),
  so the DB-level work for "no-op edits don't touch last_updated_at" is already
  done.

  I considered two earlier-numbered alternatives and set both aside for now:
  - FR-002 (Duplicate Detection) has no dependency on FR-005 at all — it's
  entirely scoped to the create workflow (FR-001, already done) and could have
  been built any time. Nothing about completing the detail view specifically
  motivates it now over any other point; it remains a reasonable candidate but
  not the one FR-005 points to.
  - FR-004 (Search and Filter) depends on the list view (FR-003, done), but its
  record-state filter (Active/Archived/All) explicitly depends on FR-009
  (Archive/Restore), which isn't built yet. The non-filter portions of FR-004
  (search, status/source/work-arrangement/date filters) could be done now, but
  the requirement as a whole is partially blocked, making it a less clean "next
  slice" than FR-006.

  FR-007 (Update Application Status) is the other strong candidate unlocked by
  FR-005, and is a very reasonable slice to follow FR-006. I'm recommending
  FR-006 first because the requirements document itself sequences it immediately
  after FR-005 and status-lifecycle management (FR-007/FR-008) reads as a
  tightly coupled pair better tackled together, later, once general-edit
  infrastructure exists.

  Dependencies on already-implemented functionality

  - FR-005 (detail view) — needed as the launch point for an "Edit" action/link,
  and its ApplicationDetail/get_application_detail query already fetches
  everything an edit form needs to pre-populate.
  - FR-001 (create_application) — its validation helpers and resolve-or-create
  logic for company/source/location are directly reusable (not duplicable) for
  the update path.
  - Persistence foundation (ADR 0001) — the AFTER UPDATE triggers with
  WHEN-guarded column comparisons already implement "genuine change advances
  last_updated_at; no-op doesn't," which is exactly what FR-006 requires and
  needs no new schema work.
  - Create Application UI patterns — the existing form-parsing helpers,
  preserved-values-on-error pattern, and ARIA-marked validation-error
  conventions in routes.py/new.html are the established template to follow for
  an edit form, per NFR-007 (maintainability/consistency).

  Ambiguities / decisions to resolve before implementing

  1. How to represent "confirmation" across a stateless HTTP request. FR-006
  requires a confirm/cancel step before a shared company-headquarters change
  commits. This needs a concrete pattern — e.g., first submission detects the
  shared change and re-renders the form as a confirmation step (with a hidden
  confirmed=1 field and the rest of the submitted data preserved) for a second
  submission — rather than a single-step save. This is the single biggest design
  decision for this slice and isn't specified by the documents; I'd want to
  settle on an approach before writing code rather than invent it silently
  mid-implementation.
  2. What "editing the Company field" actually changes. Architecture implies two
  distinct operations that both appear under the one FR-006 "Company" list
  item: (a) re-associating the application with a different (existing-or-new)
  company, resolved the same way as creation — no shared-data mutation; versus
  (b) editing that company's own hq_location_id, which does mutate shared data
  and triggers the confirmation requirement. Only company headquarters edits are
  called out as needing confirmation — not company re-association, and not
  source or job-location edits (which are also plain re-association, never
  in-place mutation of shared fields). I believe this reading is correct and not
  truly ambiguous, but it's subtle enough to state explicitly before
  implementation rather than risk it being silently misapplied.
  3. Sequencing when both the company and its headquarters change in the same 
  edit. If a user simultaneously switches an application to a different company
  and edits the headquarters field, architecture's text ("changing company
  displays the selected company's headquarters") implies the HQ edit should be
  evaluated against the newly selected company, not the original one — the
  company reassignment must resolve first, then the shared-change check runs
  against the new company. Needs to be explicit in the implementation order, not
  assumed.
  4. Whether duplicate detection (FR-002, still unimplemented) has any bearing 
  on edits. FR-002's own text scopes it to "application entry," which reads as
  creation, not editing. I'd treat edit as out of scope for duplicate detection
  unless told otherwise — flagging rather than assuming, since FR-002 remains
  unbuilt either way.
  5. Edit form template strategy — reuse the existing applications/new.html
  template (parameterized for create vs. edit) versus a dedicated
  applications/edit.html. This is an implementation-approach choice, not a
  product-behavior question, but worth deciding deliberately rather than
  defaulting to duplication.

  I have not modified any files. Awaiting confirmation of scope/approach before
  implementing FR-006.

      692 +    connection,                                               
      693 +    application_id,                                           
      694 +    *,

      696 +    job_title,                                                
      697 +    application_date: date,

      699 +    job_location: LocationInput | None = None,                
      700 +    company_hq_location: LocationInput | None = None,

          +ion_id = ?",

      721 +    source_name = _require_text("source_name", source_name)   
      722 +    if application_date is None:                              
      723 +        raise ValidationError("application_date", "is required
          +")

          +S                                                             
      727 +    )                                                         
      728 +    employment_type = _require_enum(                          
      729 +        "employment_type", employment_type, EMPLOYMENT_TYPES  
      730 +    )                                                         
      731 +    compensation_basis = _require_enum(                       
      732 +        "compensation_basis", compensation_basis, COMPENSATION
          +_BASES                                                        
      733 +    )                                                         
      734 +                                                              
      735 +    external_job_id = _trim(external_job_id) or None          
      736 +    job_url = _trim(job_url) or None                          
      737 +                                                              
      738 +    try:                                                      
      739 +        company_id, is_new_company = _resolve_or_create_compan
          +y(                                                            
      740 +            connection, company_name                          
      741 +        )                                                     
      742 +        _apply_company_headquarters_change(                   
      743 +            connection,

      745 +            is_new_company,                                   
      746 +            company_hq_location,

      748 +            confirm_shared_headquarters_change,               
      749 +        )

          +ce_name)

          +on, job_location)                                             
      752 +

      768 +                application_date = ?,                         
      769 +                notes = ?

      771 +            """,

● Review Summary

  Reviewed the Application Edit (FR-006) implementation against
  mvp-requirements.md, architecture.md, and test-strategy.md. Re-read the
  current code fresh and ran targeted empirical checks beyond the existing 25
  edit-specific tests, focused on scenarios test-strategy.md explicitly
  prioritizes ("data-integrity rules," "boundary and negative conditions"). No
  files were modified.

  High

  1. Reassigning an application's company does not refresh the headquarters 
  fields to the newly-selected company, directly violating an explicit 
  architecture.md requirement — and this is reachable through completely 
  ordinary use, with real data-corruption consequences.

  architecture.md states unambiguously: "Selecting an existing company uses its 
  existing headquarters location. Changing an application's company shall 
  therefore display the selected company's headquarters rather than carry over 
  the previous company's headquarters." The edit form doesn't implement this —
  the headquarters fields are pre-filled once (from the application's original
  company) on GET, and nothing refreshes them when the user edits the Company
  field, since there's no client-side logic and each submission is evaluated as
  a single flat form.

  Confirmed via two concrete scenarios simulating a real user who edits only the
  Company field and leaves the (pre-filled, now-stale) headquarters fields
  untouched — exactly what a browser resubmits by default:

  - Reassigning to an existing, shared company: the confirmation flow fires, but
  with the wrong data — it proposes overwriting the new company's real
  headquarters (e.g., "Chicago, IL, USA") with the old company's stale
  headquarters (e.g., "Austin, TX, USA"), which the user never intended to
  change at all. A user who doesn't scrutinize the confirmation values
  (plausible — the box just says "I understand this will change the
  headquarters...") could unknowingly corrupt a different company's shared
  headquarters data for every application referencing it.
  - Reassigning to a brand-new or unshared company: this is worse — there's no
  confirmation gate at all for new/unshared companies, so the stale carried-over
  headquarters is applied silently (confirmed: 302 immediate success). The new
  company ends up headquartered wherever the previous company happened to be — a
  value the user never chose for it, with zero warning.

  This isn't a contrived edge case; it's what happens whenever a user changes
  which company an application belongs to without separately clearing three text
  fields that give no visual cue they need attention. It also correlates with a
  test-strategy.md gap: this is precisely the "boundary and negative condition"
  / "data-integrity rule" class of scenario the strategy calls out as
  high-priority, and it isn't exercised by the 25 edit tests.

  Suggested fix direction (not implemented, for consideration): when the
  resolved company genuinely differs from the application's current company,
  don't apply the submitted company_hq_location on that same submission —
  instead redisplay the form pre-filled with the newly selected company's actual
  current headquarters and let the user explicitly edit it in a follow-up
  submission, mirroring the two-step confirmation pattern already built for the
  shared-change case.

  Low

  2. Three correct-but-untested edge cases (verified via ad-hoc scripts, not
  defects, but real gaps in the automated suite given test-strategy.md's
  risk-based coverage guidance):
  - A case/whitespace-only difference in the headquarters input (e.g., "  AUSTIN
  " vs. the stored "Austin") is correctly treated as no real change — no
  confirmation required even on a shared company, and the company's
  last_updated_at correctly stays untouched.
  - Adding a headquarters to a previously headquarters-less shared company
  correctly requires confirmation (not just changing an existing one).
  - Clearing (blanking) a headquarters on a shared company correctly requires
  confirmation, and the value is correctly left untouched when unconfirmed.

  3. Editing an archived application isn't blocked at either the service or
  route layer. Currently moot — no route sets archived_at yet, so this can't be
  reached in practice — but worth a deliberate decision once FR-009
  (archive/restore) lands, consistent with how the equivalent gap was already
  noted (and accepted) for the detail view.

  Confirmed correct — no issues found

  - All FR-006 editable fields update correctly; status is never touched by this
  operation (verified: status history unchanged, current status unaffected).
  - created_at preserved, last_updated_at advances only on a genuine change and
  stays untouched on a true no-op edit (both application- and company-level,
  confirmed for the company row too during this review).
  - Company reassignment to an existing or brand-new company works correctly
  when not compounded with the stale-headquarters issue above.
  - The two-step confirmation flow itself (raise → roll back everything →
  re-render with warning → confirmed resubmission → applies to every application
  sharing the company) works exactly as designed when the proposed headquarters
  value is the one the user actually intended.
  - Company reassignment + headquarters evaluation correctly targets the newly 
  selected company, not the old one (the ordering is right — only the data 
  flowing into that evaluation is sometimes wrong, per finding #1).
  - Validation and database-constraint failures roll back completely, including
  any company/location rows resolved earlier in the same attempt.
  - FR-002 (duplicate detection) correctly out of scope, per the confirmed
  decision.
  - No SQL injection surface; all queries parameterized or built from a fixed
  whitelist.
  - Reflected values (including the company name interpolated into the
  confirmation banner) remain correctly HTML-escaped; the
  non-finite-compensation rejection carries over correctly to the edit path.
  - The shared-macro template refactor introduced no regression in the create
  flow (confirmed via the full pre-existing create-form test suite passing
  unmodified).
  - Test levels match test-strategy.md's model: service-level tests against a
  raw connection (test_application_edit.py) plus Flask application-level tests
  via the test client (test_application_edit_routes.py).
  - No scope expansion — FR-007/008/009/004/002 and reference-data management
  remain untouched.

  Recommendation

  Finding #1 should be addressed before this slice is considered done — it's a
  genuine, ordinary-usage-reachable data-integrity gap directly contradicting
  documented architecture, not a polish item. #2 and #3 are reasonable to defer
  or fold into a later pass. I have not modified any files; let me know if you'd
  like me to implement the fix.

● Summary

  Root fix — src/job_hub/applications.py: edit_application() now fetches the
  application's current company_id before resolving the submitted company, and
  compares them. Whenever they differ (a genuine reassignment), the submitted
  company_hq_location is never applied in that same request — regardless of
  whether the target company is brand-new, unshared, or shared. A newly-created
  company gets no headquarters; an existing company's headquarters is left
  exactly as-is. _apply_company_headquarters_change (and its shared-company
  confirmation gate) is now only reached when the company is unchanged, i.e., a
  deliberate, separate edit. EditApplicationResult gained a company_reassigned
  field.

  src/job_hub/routes.py: captures the edit result and flashes an informational
  (non-blocking) message when company_reassigned is true, explaining that
  headquarters wasn't touched and can be set via a follow-up edit.

  src/job_hub/static/css/style.css: added .flash-info styling for the new
  message category.

  Verified end-to-end (not just via tests) that both original bug variants are 
  closed:
  - Reassigning to a shared existing company with stale carried-over
  headquarters no longer triggers a misleading confirmation proposing to
  overwrite that company's real headquarters — the reassignment now just
  succeeds (302), and the target company's headquarters is confirmed unchanged.
  - Reassigning to a new/unshared company with stale headquarters no longer
  silently applies it — confirmed the new company's hq_location_id is NULL after
  the reassignment.
  - The legitimate two-step workflow still works: a follow-up edit (company now
  matching, no longer a reassignment) can successfully set a new company's
  headquarters, and the existing shared-company confirmation gate still fires
  correctly on that follow-up when appropriate.

  Tests: rewrote two tests that had been asserting the old (buggy) behavior;
  added 4 new service-level tests
  (test_reassignment_never_applies_submitted_headquarters_even_to_a_new_company,
  test_reassignment_to_existing_company_never_changes_its_headquarters,
  test_reassignment_to_a_shared_company_does_not_require_confirmation,
  test_headquarters_can_be_edited_as_a_separate_followup_after_reassignment,
  test_reassigning_company_does_not_leak_previous_companys_headquarters) and 4
  route-level regression tests reproducing both original HTTP-reachable
  scenarios plus the two-step workaround and the informational flash.

  Design trade-off (documented in the journal): chosen over a more complex "show
  accurate data + require re-acknowledgement" round trip because it fully
  closes both bug variants without new hidden state, at the cost of needing two
  separate edits to reassign a company and change its headquarters in one
  conceptual action — a reasonable trade-off for a personal, single-user Phase 1
  tool.

  Test result: pytest -v → 157 passed, 0 failed (3.38s). No new dependencies.
  Nothing committed.
