  real headquarters (confirmed Chicago shown, stale Austin absent) — this is the
  mechanism the whole fix depends on, and it holds.
  - Transaction atomicity around the fix: a reassignment followed by a later
  constraint failure (compensation min>max) in the same request rolls back the
  reassignment too — verified no orphan company row and the application still
  shows its pre-edit company afterward.
  - The shared-headquarters confirmation workflow itself (untouched by this fix,
  but explicitly in scope for this review) still works correctly end-to-end:
  unconfirmed attempt → rollback, warning shown; confirmed attempt → applies to
  every application sharing that company.

  Medium: none

  Low — new findings from this review

  1. The informational "Company changed" flash fires unconditionally on every 
  reassignment, even when nothing was actually discarded (e.g., no headquarters
  fields were submitted at all, or the submitted value already matched the
  target's current headquarters). Confirmed empirically. Not a data-integrity
  issue — nothing is lost either way — but the message's wording ("Any
  headquarters submitted... was not applied") can be inaccurate/confusing when
  there was nothing to apply in the first place.
  2. Two scenarios I manually verified as correct are not covered by the 
  automated test suite: (a) a company reassignment followed by a later
  database-constraint failure correctly rolling back the reassignment itself,
  not just the reassignment-adjacent headquarters logic; (b) the GET 
  /applications/<id>/edit route showing the newly-reassigned company's accurate
  headquarters immediately after a reassignment (only the service-layer
  equivalent and a later manual-edit case are tested at the route level). Both
  pass today; neither is regression-protected.

  Low — previously identified, still deferred (unchanged by this fix, carried 
  forward for completeness)

  3. Case/whitespace-only differences in headquarters input are correctly
  treated as no real change (verified again in this review), adding a
  headquarters to a previously headquarters-less shared company correctly
  requires confirmation, and clearing a headquarters on a shared company
  correctly requires confirmation — all still correct but still untested by the
  automated suite.
  4. Editing an archived application is not blocked at either layer — still
  moot, since no route sets archived_at yet; revisit alongside FR-009.

  Confirmed correct — no new risks introduced by the fix

  - No submitted user data is silently lost or misinterpreted outside the one
  deliberate, now-disclosed case (headquarters on reassignment) — verified every
  other field (job title, application date, source, job location, description,
  URL, external ID, work arrangement, employment type, compensation, notes)
  applies normally regardless of company_reassigned, both via code inspection
  and by re-running the full non-headquarters edit tests.
  - Job location re-association carries no analogous risk (confirmed by design:
  it only repoints the application's own FK, never mutates a shared record —
  unlike company.hq_location_id), so the fix is correctly scoped to just the one
  field FR-006 itself singles out.
  - Validation and error handling are unaffected: non-finite compensation still
  rejected, blank required fields still rejected with correct field-level
  aria-invalid marking, oversized/non-integer application IDs still 404
  (not 500) on the edit route too.
  - XSS escaping and the informational flash's accessibility (role="status" 
  aria-live="polite", correctly HTML-escaped) all verified intact.
  - Create-form regression safety: the shared _form_macros.html extraction is
  unaffected by this fix (it wasn't touched), and the full pre-existing
  create-form suite remains green.
  - No scope expansion, no new dependencies (pyproject.toml diff empty), file
  set matches exactly what's expected for this slice.
  - Journal entry accurately describes the fix, the scenarios it closes, the
  design trade-off, and the resulting test count (157) — verified accurate
  against the actual current test count.

  Verdict

  Ready to commit. The high-severity finding is genuinely and thoroughly fixed —
  verified independently across atomicity, the escape-hatch mechanism, and both

  No new data-integrity risks were introduced, and no submitted user data is

● Next Slice: FR-007 — Update Application Status

  Requirement

  FR-007 — Update Application Status (docs/mvp-requirements.md)

  ▎ The system shall allow the current status of an application to be changed.

  Acceptance criteria, as documented:

  - A status change requires: new status, status effective date and time.
  - A status change may include status-specific notes.
  - Recording a status change creates a new APPLICATION_STATUS_HISTORY record;
  existing history is never overwritten.
  - The newly recorded status becomes the application's current status only when
  its effective date/time is the most recent among all history for that
  application — not because it was just entered.
  - The distinction between effective date/time and the history record's own
  created_at (when it was entered into the system) must be preserved.
  - The user can cancel a status change without modifying history.
  - Status effective date/time shall not be in the future.
  - Status changes may be entered retrospectively; when they are, current status
  is still determined purely by the most recent effective_at, not by insertion
  order.
  - Two history records for the same application shall not share the same
  effective date/time.

  Supporting architecture.md text ("Status Lifecycle Behavior" section — the
  same section that also specifies FR-008's correction/deletion rules,
  confirming these two are documented as a pair): "Status changes append history
  rather than overwrite existing events. Backdated events are permitted; future
  effective timestamps are prohibited. Adding an older event does not displace 
  a later effective event as current status."

  Why this is the appropriate next slice

  Roadmap.md's Phase 1 "Product Goals" list names "Track each opportunity 
  through a defined status lifecycle" and "Update opportunity information and 
  status" as core, near-top goals — notably, archiving is not mentioned anywhere
  in that list. FR-006 just closed "update opportunity information"; FR-007 is
  the other half of that same roadmap bullet, and the app currently has a real,
  glaring gap: it can create an application with an initial status and display
  full status history, but has no way for a user to ever record a status change
  after creation. For a job-application tracker, the ability to watch an
  application progress (APPLIED → SCREENING → INTERVIEWING → OFFER/REJECTED) is
  arguably the single most central use case — without it, the tracker can create
  records but can't reflect the actual job search as it unfolds.

  It's also unusually well-supported by what already exists: the
  application_status_history schema (including the UNIQUE(application_id, 
  effective_at) constraint and the no-op-safe last_updated_at trigger), the
  STATUS reference table, and — critically — the "current status" derivation
  (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY effective_at DESC))
  used identically by both the list and detail views require zero changes.
  Adding a new, later-dated history row is automatically picked up as "current"
  everywhere it's displayed, with no new derivation logic to write — a direct
  payoff of the "single consistent derivation, no cache" design already
  documented in architecture.md.

  I considered FR-009 (Archive/Restore) as the other strong candidate — it's
  simpler to implement and the archived_at column has been sitting ready since
  the persistence-foundation slice (and get_application_detail was deliberately
  built not to filter by it, anticipating this). But archiving is absent from
  roadmap.md's Phase 1 goal list entirely, and it's more of a list-hygiene
  feature than a core lifecycle capability. I'm recommending FR-007 first to
  keep the "core application lifecycle" arc (Create → List → Detail → Edit →
  Status Update → Status Correction) coherent before branching into
  archive/restore and search/filter, which are more about managing a growing
  list than completing the lifecycle model itself.

  Dependencies on already-implemented functionality

  - FR-005 (detail view) — the natural launch point for a "Change Status"
  action, and it already displays the complete status history and computed
  current_status_name, giving the user full context before choosing a new
  status.
  - FR-001's status-history persistence — the schema, the _format_timestamp
  convention, and the general pattern of inserting a history row are directly
  reusable; only the effective-at validation needs adapting, since FR-007 has no
  equivalent to FR-001's "defaults to now if status is APPLIED and date is
  today" shortcut — a status change always requires an explicit effective
  date/time (no conditional default to invent).
  - The current-status derivation (list, detail) — requires no changes at all; a
  new history row is picked up automatically.
  - Established Flask patterns from FR-001/FR-006 — form parsing,
  validation-error/ARIA conventions, the commit-or-rollback transaction wrapper,
  and the "detail page action → form → redirect back to detail" navigation
  shape all carry over directly.
  - No schema changes needed — same as FR-006, this is purely an
  application/route/template-layer addition.

  What later functionality depends on this

  - FR-008 (Correct Application Status History) — not a hard technical
  dependency (FR-008 could technically operate on FR-001's initial-only
  history), but a strong product-coherence one: "fix a status change" is a
  natural, closely-paired follow-on to "make a status change," and their UI
  would likely live side by side on the detail page's history table.
  - Later Phase 2 roadmap items (dashboards, summary information, "improved
  sorting and filtering" by status) depend on status history actually being
  populated with real transitions over time, not just a single initial entry.
  - FR-004's status filter becomes materially more useful once applications can
  actually carry varied, evolving statuses in practice (not a hard dependency,
  but a "why bother filtering by status yet" consideration).

  Ambiguities / decisions to resolve before implementation

  1. Route naming/shape — following the /applications/<id>/edit precedent, I'd
  propose /applications/<id>/status (or /change-status) for the
  new-status-change form. Not specified anywhere; worth confirming rather than
  silently picking.
  2. Default selection in the "new status" dropdown. Unlike FR-001's create flow
  (defaults to APPLIED), there's no documented "logical next status." I'd
  default to no selection (forcing an explicit, deliberate choice) rather than
  invent a display-order-based "suggested next status" the docs don't call for.
  3. Re-selecting the current status. FR-007 doesn't forbid recording a new
  history entry with the same status as current (e.g., a note like "still
  waiting" with a fresh timestamp) — I'd treat this as legitimate, not something
  to block, since nothing in the documented rules restricts it.
  4. UNIQUE(application_id, effective_at) collisions. Following the established
  pattern (compensation min>max on create/edit), I'd let this surface as a plain
  database-constraint rejection rather than duplicating that check in Python —
  worth confirming this is still the preferred approach for this slice.
  5. Status changes on an archived application. Currently moot (no route sets
  archived_at yet, consistent with the same open question already noted for
  FR-005/FR-006) — revisit once FR-009 exists.
  6. Retrospective/backdated entries not becoming "current." This is actually
  not ambiguous — FR-007 and architecture.md are explicit that a backdated
  status change must not displace a later-effective status as current — but it's
  worth calling out explicitly since it's the one behavior most likely to be
  gotten wrong if implemented carelessly (e.g., naively treating "most recently
  inserted" as "current").

  I have not modified any files. Awaiting confirmation of scope/approach before
  implementing FR-007.

● Now implementing the fix. Root cause: create_application's default now is
  constructed as UTC-aware, then compared via now.date() against
  application_date (which the form derives from local date.today()). Near
  UTC-day-boundary hours in negative-offset timezones, these disagree. The fix
  is to make the default now local-aware — _format_timestamp already correctly
  normalizes any aware datetime to UTC for storage, so this only affects the "is
  today" comparison, not what gets persisted.

● Summary

  Root cause: create_application's default now (used on every real request,
  since Flask routes never pass now explicitly) was constructed as
  datetime.now(timezone.utc), then compared via now.date() against
  application_date — a value with no timezone of its own, populated from the
  create form's date.today() (local). This is a frame mismatch: for roughly four
  hours daily in negative-UTC-offset timezones (like EDT), UTC's calendar day
  is already ahead of local, so an ordinary "create an application for today
  with the default APPLIED status" submission incorrectly demanded an explicit
  effective time it shouldn't need.

  Fix (src/job_hub/applications.py): changed the default to
  datetime.now().astimezone() — the current moment as an aware datetime in the
  system's local timezone, matching what the form's date.today() default means.
  _format_timestamp already normalizes any aware datetime to UTC before storage
  regardless of its original tzinfo, so persisted timestamps are completely 
  unaffected — only the "is this today" comparison changes. The comparison logic
  itself was never wrong; only the default it was fed was.

  Scope discipline: change_application_status's default now (added for FR-007)
  uses the same datetime.now(timezone.utc) pattern but has no equivalent bug —
  it's only used for future-timestamp rejection, and aware-datetime comparisons
  are timezone-correct regardless of which zone now is expressed in. Left
  unchanged rather than "fixed for consistency," since nothing there is actually
  broken.

  Tests added (tests/test_applications.py):
  - test_default_now_uses_local_today_not_utc_today — omits the now override
  entirely, exercising the real default against the real local date.today().
  This reliably failed during the affected window with the old code and reliably
  passes now, regardless of time of day.
  - test_today_comparison_respects_nows_own_timezone_not_utc — fully
  deterministic, using an explicit UTC-5 now where the UTC and local calendar
  days differ, proving the underlying comparison was already correct given a
  properly local-aware value.

  Verification: confirmed directly against the real system clock at fix time
  (local 8:59 PM EDT / UTC 12:59 AM next day — still within the affected window)
  that the old expression reproduces the mismatch and the new one matches real
  local date.today() exactly. All 36 previously-failing tests now pass at the

● Final Review Summary

  Re-read FR-007's acceptance criteria, the relevant architecture.md sections,
  test-strategy.md, the implementation, tests, and journal fresh. Ran the full
  suite (189 passed) and a substantial battery of independent empirical checks
  beyond what the automated tests assert. No files were modified.

  Medium — new finding

  The two new timezone-fix regression tests do not, between them, provide 
  deterministic protection against reintroduction of the actual bug — confirmed 
  by direct experiment, not just inspection.

  - test_default_now_uses_local_today_not_utc_today omits now, exercising the
  real default at whatever moment the test runs. I confirmed it fails under the
  old buggy expression right now — but only because real time happens to be
  inside the ~4-hour daily UTC/local-offset window. Outside that window, this
  test would pass identically under the old and new code, giving false
  confidence.
  - test_today_comparison_respects_nows_own_timezone_not_utc explicitly passes
  now=local_now. I traced the actual code path: now or 
  datetime.now().astimezone() short-circuits on the truthy explicit value, so
  the default expression — old or new — is never evaluated in this test at all.
  It would pass identically whether the fix was applied or reverted. This is
  exactly the failure mode the task asked me to check for: this test "merely
  confirms the implementation" (that the comparison logic handles a good now
  correctly, which was never broken) rather than "genuinely exercising the
  defect" (the broken default construction).

  Net effect: there is currently no test that reliably catches a future
  reintroduction of this exact bug regardless of time of day. A deterministic
  fix would need to mock datetime.now (feasible via stdlib unittest.mock.patch,
  no new dependency) rather than rely on wall-clock timing. The underlying fix 
  itself is correct — I independently verified it (below) — this finding is
  specifically about test-suite reliability, not the fix's correctness.

  Low — new finding

  A timezone-naive now is interpreted inconsistently depending on how it 
  arrives. When now is omitted, the new default (datetime.now().astimezone()) is
  local-aware. But if a caller explicitly passes a naive now (bypassing the
  default via now or ...), the pre-existing safety net (if now.tzinfo is None: 
  now = now.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)) still coerces it to UTC — a different
  interpretation of "naive" than the omitted-argument case. Confirmed
  empirically. Currently unreachable: no caller in the codebase (routes or
  tests) ever passes a naive now. Worth a short comment for future maintainers,
  not urgent.

  Confirmed correct — FR-001 timezone fix

  - UTC storage normalization holds: verified directly against the real system
  clock (local 9:02 PM EDT / UTC 1:02 AM next day) that the stored effective_at
  for a real, unforced create_application() call correctly matches the real UTC
  moment (2026-09-21T01:02:32...Z), not the local date/time — the local-aware
  default only changes the "is this today" comparison, never what gets
  persisted.
  - No timezone-naive comparison is introduced: datetime.now() (naive) is
  immediately resolved to aware via .astimezone() before any comparison touches
  it — confirmed by direct inspection and by testing the exact
  naive-now-safety-net interaction above.
  - The comparison logic itself was never the bug — confirmed empirically that a
  properly local-aware now produces correct results even under the old code;
  only the default's timezone was wrong.
  - All 36 previously-failing tests pass now, at real times that were failing
  minutes before the fix was applied.

  Confirmed correct — FR-007

  Independently re-verified (not just re-running existing tests) against every
  item requested:
  - Append-only history: change_application_status only ever INSERTs; no
  UPDATE/DELETE touches existing rows or the application table.
  - Explicit status selection: confirmed via template inspection — the blank
  option is always the one marked selected on load; blank submission raises
  status_name: is required.
  - Repeated same-status events: accepted as a legitimate new history entry with
  its own timestamp/notes.
  - effective_at vs. created_at: confirmed distinct and correctly populated per
  history row.
  - Backdated events / current-status derivation: re-verified — a backdated
  entry is recorded in correct chronological order but does not become current
  when a later-effective entry already exists; required zero new derivation
  code, reusing the existing shared ROW_NUMBER()-based logic.
  - Future timestamps / duplicate effective_at: both rejected correctly;
  duplicate-timestamp rejection surfaces as the established generic
  sqlite3.IntegrityError → error pattern.
  - Cancellation/no-op: confirmed empirically that repeated GETs of the
  status-change form produce zero writes.
  - Transaction rollback: confirmed the connection remains fully usable for a
  subsequent call after a failed (duplicate-timestamp) status change.
  - archived_at untouched: confirmed via direct query after a status change.
  - application.last_updated_at untouched by status changes (correctly separate
  from the history row's own timestamps) — verified directly, a detail not
  explicitly called out before but worth confirming given FR-007 and FR-006 sit
  right next to each other in the schema.
  - Accessibility: role="alert" on errors, aria-invalid via the shared macro,
  correct label/for association — consistent with the rest of the application.
  - Navigation: "Change Status" link from detail, "Cancel" link back to detail,
  both present and correct.
  - Reflected notes content is escaped (verified with a script-tag payload);
  oversized/non-integer application IDs 404 rather than 500, via the same
  established OverflowError handling.
  - No scope expansion: the diff is confined to exactly what FR-007 and the
  timezone fix require — no dependency changes (pyproject.toml diff empty), no
  incidental changes elsewhere.

  Pre-existing/deferred observations (unchanged by this diff, restated for 
  completeness only)

  From earlier reviews, still Low, still not part of this change set: FR-005's
  "Back to Applications" list-state loss on navigate-back; FR-006's
  untested-but-correct case/whitespace-equivalent-headquarters and
  add/clear-headquarters-on-shared-company scenarios; editing/status-changing an
  archived application isn't blocked (moot until FR-009 exists).

  Verdict

  Ready to commit. The FR-001 timezone fix is genuinely correct — verified
  independently through direct empirical checks of storage normalization and
  comparison semantics, not just by trusting the two added tests. FR-007
  correctly implements every requested acceptance criterion, with no regressions
  and no scope creep. The one Medium finding is a test-suite reliability gap
  (the regression tests don't deterministically guard the fix), not a defect in
  the shipped behavior — reasonable to address as a fast follow-up rather than
  block this commit.

● Next Slice: FR-008 — Correct Application Status History

  Requirement

  FR-008 — Correct Application Status History (docs/mvp-requirements.md)

  ▎ The system shall allow an existing application status-history record to be 
  ▎ corrected when information was entered incorrectly.

  Acceptance criteria, as documented:

  - The user can edit: Status, Status effective date and time, Status-specific
  notes.
  - A corrected effective date/time shall not be in the future.
  - A correction shall not result in two history records for the same
  application sharing an effective date/time.
  - Correcting a record preserves its original created_at and updates its
  last_updated_at.
  - After a correction, current status is recalculated using the most recent
  remaining effective_at.
  - Deleting a history record requires confirmation.
  - Deleting a record causes current status to be recalculated from what
  remains.
  - An application shall always contain at least one history record — deletion
  of the only remaining one is prohibited.
  - The user can cancel a correction without changing persisted data.

  Architecture.md's "Status Lifecycle Behavior" section documents FR-007 and
  FR-008 in one continuous passage, not as separately-scoped concerns: "Status 
  changes append history... Corrections may change a history record's status, 
  effective timestamp, or notes, while preserving created_at... Deleting a 
  history record requires confirmation and shall be rejected if it would remove 
  the application's only remaining record. After correction or deletion, current
  status follows the greatest remaining effective_at." This is the strongest
  textual signal available that these two requirements were designed as one
  cohesive capability, not independent slices that happen to be numbered
  consecutively.

  Why this is the appropriate next slice — and why FR-007 specifically makes it 
  so now

  You asked me to weigh this directly: yes, FR-008 is now the right next slice, 
  and FR-007's completion is the specific reason, not just numerical proximity.

  Before FR-007, every application had exactly one status-history record — the
  one FR-001 creates at submission time. FR-008 would have been technically
  buildable against that alone, but the capability would have been narrow: the
  only correctable/deletable record was the single initial entry, and "deletion
  of the only remaining record is prohibited" would have had no real contrast to
  test (every application was always in that state). FR-007 changes this
  materially: applications can now accumulate a genuine, growing sequence of
  status-history entries through ordinary, frequent use — and FR-007 has no 
  confirmation or review step before committing a status change (unlike FR-006's
  shared-headquarters gate). That combination — frequent entry, no safety net —
  makes data-entry mistakes (wrong status selected, wrong date typed, wrong
  notes) a realistic, recurring event for the first time. FR-008 is what lets a
  user recover from those mistakes, and it's now testable in its full, intended
  form: correcting/deleting one entry among several, with current-status
  recalculation actually having something to recalculate from.

  Practically, FR-008 also reuses everything FR-007 just built with minimal new
  surface area: the same future-date rejection, the same status lookup, the same
  DB-enforced uniqueness constraint, and the same "current status is always
  derived, never cached" guarantee that requires zero new derivation code for an
  UPDATE or DELETE any more than it did for FR-007's INSERT.

  I re-considered FR-009 (Archive/Restore) and FR-004 (Search/Filter) as
  alternatives, consistent with how I evaluated them before FR-007. Neither is
  newly motivated by FR-007's completion the way FR-008 is — FR-009 remains
  absent from roadmap.md's Phase 1 "Product Goals" bullet list entirely, and
  FR-004's most-blocked piece (record-state filtering) still depends on FR-009,
  which doesn't exist yet. FR-002 (duplicate detection) is scoped to the create
  workflow and is similarly unaffected by anything FR-007 introduced. FR-008 is
  the one requirement whose value and testability was directly and specifically
  increased by the work that just landed.

  Dependencies on already-implemented functionality

  - FR-005 (detail view) — already renders the complete, ordered status-history
  table with each entry's ID, status, effective_at, notes, and current-status
  marker; this is exactly where "Correct"/"Delete" actions per row belong.
  - FR-007's validation helpers (_reject_future_effective_at, the
  now-parametrized _resolve_status_id) — directly reusable for the correction
  path with no duplication.
  - Persistence foundation — UNIQUE(application_id, effective_at) and the
  history table's own no-op-safe last_updated_at trigger already implement
  exactly the "preserve created_at, update last_updated_at only on a genuine
  change" requirement FR-008 calls for. No schema changes needed, same as FR-006
  and FR-007.
  - Current-status derivation — the shared ROW_NUMBER()-based logic recalculates
  automatically after any change to application_status_history; FR-008 needs no
  new derivation code, only correctly wired UPDATE/DELETE operations.
  - The "at least one record" invariant is already established by FR-001 (every
  application is created with one history row); FR-008 adds the explicit guard
  against deleting the last one.

  What depends on this

  Nothing is structurally blocked by FR-008's absence, but it closes out the
  "Status Lifecycle Behavior" architecture section entirely, and any future
  reporting/analytics on status history (Phase 2 roadmap items) benefits from
  that history being correctable rather than permanently accumulating
  uncorrectable mistakes once FR-007 makes frequent entry the norm.

  Ambiguities / decisions to resolve before implementation

  1. Route shape for correcting vs. deleting a specific history entry — e.g.,
  /applications/<id>/status/<history_id>/edit and a separate delete action,
  following the established per-resource pattern. Not specified; needs a
  concrete decision.
  2. How deletion confirmation is represented across the stateless HTTP flow.
  Given this project's consistent avoidance of client-side JS confirmation
  dialogs, I'd expect a dedicated confirm step (GET renders a "delete this
  entry?" page, POST performs it) rather than FR-006's more complex two-step
  data-comparison pattern — deletion here has no equivalent "shared data"
  complexity to detect. Worth confirming rather than assuming.
  3. Should the correction form pre-fill the entry's existing values, or start 
  blank like FR-007's new-status form? I'd say pre-fill (matching FR-006's
  edit-form precedent — correcting a mistake is naturally an "edit," not a fresh
  choice), unlike FR-007's deliberate blank-by-default for a new status change.
  This is a real design choice, not a technicality, and shouldn't be silently
  assumed either way.
  4. Correcting/deleting the current entry is explicitly allowed — FR-008's text
  doesn't carve out an exception, and doing so correctly falls back to the
  next-most-recent remaining entry per the existing derivation. Stating this
  clearly now since it's an easy point to get wrong if someone assumes the
  current entry is special-cased.
  5. The "last remaining record" delete guard should be enforced at both layers
  — hidden/disabled in the UI when only one record exists, and independently
  re-enforced in the service layer, consistent with this project's established
  "DB/service layer is the final integrity boundary" discipline.
  6. application.last_updated_at should remain untouched by correction or
  deletion, exactly as already verified for FR-007's status changes — stating
  this explicitly as the expected, already-precedented behavior rather than
  something to re-derive.

  I have not modified any files or implemented anything. Awaiting confirmation
  of scope/approach before proceeding with FR-008.

  functionality. Do not commit.

● FR-008 Review

  I checked the implementation against mvp-requirements.md's FR-008 text,
  architecture.md's "Status Lifecycle Behavior" / "Transaction Boundaries"
  sections, and test-strategy.md. I re-derived and verified several behaviors
  directly against the running code (not just by reading) rather than assuming
  the earlier smoke tests covered everything.

  Confirmed correct and compliant:
  - Transaction boundary for delete: the "at least one record remains" check and
  the DELETE occur inside the same commit/rollback-guarded block, per
  architecture.md's explicit requirement that this check and the deletion happen
  in the same protected transaction.
  - created_at preservation / last_updated_at update on correction — verified
  directly (not just by reading the trigger): corrected a record after a 1s
  sleep, confirmed created_at unchanged and last_updated_at advanced.
  - Current-status recalculation after both correction and deletion, including
  the current-entry case, falls out of the existing derivation query with no
  special-casing, as intended.
  - Deletion requires a GET-confirm-then-POST step; no write transaction is held
  open during confirmation.
  - Cross-application ID confusion (application A's URL with application B's
  history_id) — verified via a live scratch test: returns 404 on GET/POST for
  both correct and delete, and B's data is untouched.
  - No dangling FK references from deleted history rows (nothing else references
  application_status_history_id).

  Findings:

  1. Medium — untested requirement: created_at/last_updated_at behavior on 
  correction. FR-008 explicitly states correction "shall preserve the record's
  original created_at timestamp and update its last_updated_at timestamp" —
  referring to the history row itself, not the application row. The current test
  suite only asserts application.last_updated_at is untouched; nothing asserts
  the history row's own created_at/last_updated_at behavior. I confirmed
  manually that production behavior is correct, but it's the one directly-worded
  FR-008 sentence with no regression test protecting it.
  2. Medium — missing regression coverage for cross-application isolation on 
  delete. correct_status_history has a service-level test proving a history_id
  belonging to a different application is rejected (returns None).
  delete_status_history has no equivalent test, and neither operation has a
  route-level test for this scenario. I verified by hand that both routes and
  delete_status_history correctly 404/no-op in this case, but this IDOR-style
  guard — arguably the more consequential one, since delete is destructive — is
  currently unprotected against regression on 3 of 4 relevant paths
  (delete-service, correct-route, delete-route).

  Both are test-coverage gaps against explicitly-stated
  requirements/architecture text, not production defects — I verified the actual
  runtime behavior is correct in each case. No High or Critical findings.

  Want me to add the two missing regression tests (no production code changes
  needed)?

● Recommendation: FR-009 (Archive and Restore an Application) next

  Of the three remaining functional slices (FR-002 Duplicate Detection, FR-004
  Search/Filter, FR-009 Archive/Restore), FR-009 should come next.

  Why FR-009, not FR-004

  Architecture.md's "Archiving and Restoration" section explicitly folds FR-009
  into FR-004's mechanics: "Archived and All record-state filters expose 
  historical applications using the same search, filter, sort, and pagination 
  behavior... Mixed lists visually distinguish archived records." FR-004's own
  text confirms this — its record-state filter (Active/Archived/All) is one of
  FR-004's defined behaviors, not a separate feature.

  The problem: nothing in the system can currently produce an archived
  application. list_applications hardcodes WHERE a.archived_at IS NULL with no
  parameter to relax it (confirmed by re-reading applications.py), and no route
  sets archived_at. Building FR-004's full search/filter UI now would mean
  either shipping a record-state filter with no data to ever show, or quietly
  deferring just that one FR-004 sub-requirement — an awkward, incoherent split.
  Implementing FR-009 first means FR-004, when it lands, can implement
  record-state filtering as a complete, testable, demonstrable feature from day
  one, using real archived data.

  Why FR-009, not FR-002

  FR-002 (duplicate warning at entry) is fully self-contained — it only touches
  the create-application flow, and nothing else in Phase 1 depends on it or is
  blocked by its absence. That makes it low-risk to defer: it can be implemented
  at any point, including last, without creating awkward half-finished
  dependent features. It's also lower incremental value right now: it's a
  data-quality safeguard against a mistake (re-entering the same application),
  whereas FR-009 addresses a capability gap that exists the moment this becomes
  a real, lived-in tracker — every application eventually reaches a terminal
  status (ACCEPTED/REJECTED/WITHDRAWN/CLOSED) and there is currently no way to
  get it out of the active list. That's the single biggest missing capability
  for actual daily use of the tool as built so far.

  Dependencies

  Already implemented, ready to build on: the archived_at column, its no-op-safe
  last_updated_at trigger, and the list view's archived_at IS NULL exclusion
  all exist already (from the SQLite persistence foundation slice) — FR-009
  mostly needs to add the write path and a way back to view archived rows. The
  detail view (FR-005) doesn't filter by archived_at at all, by earlier explicit
  design ("a detail page reachable by ID should not depend on archive state") —
  so it's already a safe place to host an Archive/Restore action and to view an
  archived application's full information.

  What FR-009 unblocks: a complete, coherent FR-004 (record-state filtering has
  real data to operate on); and it closes the loop on FR-003/architecture.md's
  already-stated "default list is active-only" design, which currently has no
  way to ever be exercised end-to-end.

  Decisions to resolve before implementing

  1. Minimal archived-application visibility. FR-009's own text requires
  archived applications to "remain available through an archived-application
  view or filter" — this can't be pure FR-004. I'd recommend adding a minimal
  record-state toggle now (e.g., a query param on the existing list route/query,
  reusing the same sort/pagination code path per architecture.md's explicit
  guidance), scoped to just Active/Archived/All — no free-text search, no
  category filters, all of which stay deferred to FR-004. This keeps FR-009
  self-contained while making the later FR-004 a natural extension rather than a
  rewrite.
  2. Confirmation shape. The requirement text says archiving explicitly requires
  confirmation; restoring has no equivalent sentence (only "the user shall be
  able to cancel an archive or restore operation," which a single non-committing
  GET/link trivially satisfies). Recommend: archive uses a
  GET-confirm-page-then-POST flow (FR-008's precedent — the target is already
  fully identified by URL, nothing needs discovering, so FR-006's heavier
  mid-transaction pattern isn't warranted); restore is a single-action
  link/button with no separate confirm page. Worth confirming this asymmetry is
  intended before building it.
  3. Where the actions live. Recommend "Archive" as a new link on the detail
  page alongside Edit/Change Status/etc.; "Restore" available both from the
  minimal archived list view and directly on an archived application's own
  detail page.
  4. Interaction with FR-002 (still deferred). Not a blocker, but worth noting:
  duplicate detection's matching logic will eventually need a decision about
  whether archived applications count as potential duplicates. Not this slice's
  concern, just flagging it as a future consideration.

  I have not modified or implemented anything. Let me know if you'd like me to
  proceed with FR-009 under this scope, or want to adjust any of the four
  decisions above first.

● FR-009 is implemented and tested. Summary of what was built:

  Service layer (applications.py) — archive_application/restore_application
  (both true no-ops when already in the target state, reusing the existing
  archived_at column and no-op-safe trigger with zero schema changes), plus
  list_applications extended with a record_state parameter (active/archived/all,
  default active) and archived_at/is_archived added to both ApplicationListItem
  and ApplicationDetail.

  Routes — GET/POST /applications/<id>/archive (confirm-then-commit) and POST 
  /applications/<id>/restore (single action, no confirm page — matching FR-009's
  own asymmetric confirmation wording); /applications gained a ?state= param.

  Templates — new archive_confirm.html; detail.html gained an archived notice
  plus Archive/Restore controls; list.html gained a minimal Active/Archived/All
  filter nav, archived-row visual distinction, and a state-aware empty message;
  style.css got the supporting classes.

  Tests — 40 new tests (13 service-level, 21 route-level, 6 extending the
  existing list test file) covering timestamp behavior, no-op idempotency, 404s,
  confirmation flow, POST-only restore, record-state
  filtering/sorting/pagination, visual distinction, and fallback for an invalid
  state value.

  Journal updated with the slice's rationale and scope. Full suite: 279 passed,
  no regressions. FR-004's free-text search/category filters and FR-002 remain
  untouched, as scoped. Nothing committed.

  - No lifecycle-status or status-history side effects from archive/restore —
  confirmed by code inspection (only archived_at is touched) and by the
  glossary's explicit "archiving does not change lifecycle status or status
  history."
  - No restriction added on editing/status-changing an archived application —
  correctly not implemented, since nothing in requirements or architecture asks
  for it.
  - record_state query-param handling is injection-safe — verified empirically
  with a SQL injection payload (?state=active'; DROP TABLE application; --); it
  falls back to the default state and the table is untouched, because the value
  is validated as a dict-key membership check before ever reaching SQL.
  - The no-op idempotency guards (re-archiving an archived application,
  re-restoring an active one) and the created_at/last_updated_at behavior are
  genuinely protected, not just asserted: I broke each production behavior in
  isolation (removed the idempotency guard; dropped the last_updated_at trigger)

● Recommendation: FR-002 (Detect Potential Duplicate Applications) next

  Yes — FR-002 is the appropriate next slice, ahead of FR-004 (the only other
  substantive remaining functional requirement).

  Why FR-002, not FR-004

  FR-004's full search/filter feature (free-text search,
  status/source/work-arrangement/employment-type/job-location/date-range filters
  with AND/OR combination) is the natural continuation of FR-009's record-state
  work — the codebase is primed for it, and I said as much when building
  FR-009. But "primed for" isn't the same as "next in line." Nothing technically
  blocks either FR-002 or FR-004 from being built in either order; this is a
  product-sequencing choice, not a dependency chain, and on that basis FR-002
  has the stronger case right now:

  - FR-002 is fully self-contained and bounded. It touches only the
  create-application workflow (FR-001's route/service), with a well-defined
  confirmation-flow precedent already established (FR-006's two-step HTTP
  pattern). FR-004 is a materially larger UI surface — multiple filter controls,
  category-combination logic, and a genuinely open design question for
  filtering by job location (a normalized city/state/country reference, not a
  plain string) that FR-002 has no equivalent of.
  - FR-002 protects data integrity at the point of entry, which matters more the
  earlier it's added — every application recorded before this slice is a window
  where an accidental duplicate could have been created undetected. FR-004 is a
  convenience/findability feature whose value scales with the number of
  applications already on file; for a personal tracker that's still accumulating
  records, preventing bad data now is higher-leverage than making a still-small
  list more searchable.
  - FR-009 just made a real design question for FR-002 concrete. Before
  archive/restore existed, "should duplicate detection also scan archived
  applications" wasn't even askable — there was no such thing as an archived
  application. Now there is, and it's a genuine decision this slice needs (see
  below). That's a small but real argument that FR-009 → FR-002 is itself a
  coherent sequence, not just "FR-002 was always available."
  - The interpretation question that mattered most was already settled, during
  FR-006: FR-002's own text scopes it to "application entry," and it was
  explicitly confirmed then that this means create only, not edit — reducing
  this slice's remaining ambiguity to implementation-shape questions rather than
  scope questions.

  Dependencies

  Already implemented, ready to build on: the FR-001 create-application
  route/form (the injection point for the warning); the two-step HTTP
  confirmation pattern from FR-006 (SharedHeadquartersChangeRequiresConfirmation
  → catch → re-render with a warning banner and explicit confirmation control →
  resubmit) as the direct template, since architecture.md's own "Application
  Duplicate Detection" section describes exactly this shape ("the user can
  review a possible duplicate and cancel or explicitly proceed... the database
  shall allow the confirmed application to be saved"); the existing
  normalized-matching infrastructure (_resolve_or_create_company's
  case/whitespace-insensitive lookup) for the company half of the duplicate
  signal; external_job_id and job_title already captured on every application
  since FR-001.

  What depends on FR-002: nothing later in Phase 1 — it's a leaf feature. That
  also means there's no risk in the ordering either way; the case above is about
  coherent value delivery, not unblocking anything downstream.

  Decisions to resolve before implementation

  1. Matching rule when no external job ID is available. Requirements only give
  "company and job title" as an example, not an exact rule. I'd recommend:
  normalized company match AND normalized (exact, case/whitespace-insensitive)
  job-title match — both required, no fuzzy/partial matching. This keeps the
  signal deterministic and avoids introducing fuzzy-matching
  complexity/libraries the architecture doesn't call for ("prefer simple
  solutions").
  2. Should duplicate scanning include archived applications, not just active 
  ones? Not addressed by requirements or architecture. I'd recommend yes — the
  point is "have I already tracked this job," and a
  rejected/withdrawn/closed-but-archived application is still evidence of a
  prior application to the same role. This is the one genuinely new decision
  FR-009 introduced.
  3. Confirmation-flow shape, following FR-006's precedent directly: the first
  submission that matches an existing application doesn't save; it re-renders
  the create form with a warning banner naming the matching application(s) and
  an explicit "Save anyway" checkbox; only a resubmission with that flag set
  persists. Recommend against a lighter JS-driven live-check given the project's
  "minimal JavaScript" stance and no existing AJAX infrastructure.
  4. What to show about each match, so the user can meaningfully "review the
  potential duplicate" per the requirement text — recommend company, job title,
  application date, current status, and a link to that application's detail
  page.
  5. Multiple matches — recommend showing all matches found rather than just the
  first, given expected personal-scale data volumes.

  Two smaller, unrelated loose ends worth naming but not recommending as the 
  next slice: FR-011's "syntactically valid web URL when supplied" validation is
  still unimplemented (explicitly deferred since the original Create
  Application slice, and still listed as an open enforcement responsibility in
  architecture.md's constraints table) — a small, targeted addition rather than
  a functional slice, but worth bundling in whenever the create form is touched
  next. Separately, FR-010's "the user shall be able to select an existing
  company, location, or source" is only satisfied at the data level (normalized
  reuse happens silently server-side) — there's no actual selection UI (e.g.,
  autocomplete), so a user has to already know the exact prior spelling to
  trigger reuse. Neither is what I'd recommend building next, but both are real,
  documented gaps worth keeping on the radar.

  I have not modified or implemented anything. Let me know if you'd like me to
  proceed with FR-002 under this scope, or adjust any of the five decisions
  above first.

● FR-002 (Detect Potential Duplicate Applications) is implemented and tested.
  Summary:

  Service layer (applications.py) — PotentialDuplicateApplicationsDetected
  exception carrying a list of PotentialDuplicateMatch records;
  _find_potential_duplicates implementing the matching rule from architecture.md
  (company + external job ID when available, else company + job title, both
  normalized case/whitespace-insensitively); wired into create_application via a
  new confirm_duplicate flag, checked before any reference-data resolution or
  transaction start (so a warned-but-unconfirmed attempt creates zero orphan
  rows). Also extracted the current-status CTE into a shared _CURRENT_STATUS_CTE
  constant, now reused by both the list query and the new duplicate query.

  Routes — new_application catches the new exception and re-renders the create
  form with the matches instead of saving.

  Template (new.html) — a warning banner listing each match (job title, company,
  application date, status, archived label) with a target="_blank" link to
  review it without losing the in-progress form, plus a "save anyway" checkbox
  that only appears when a warning is present.

  Decisions applied exactly as proposed: archived applications are included in
  the duplicate scan (a new consideration now that FR-009 exists); the
  external-ID and job-title indicators are mutually exclusive (job-title
  fallback only applies when the new entry has no external ID); editing never
  triggers the check, consistent with the interpretation already settled during
  FR-006.

  Tests — 27 new (17 service-level, 10 route-level) covering both matching
  indicators, normalization, the exclusivity edge case, archived-application
  matches, the confirm-and-resubmit flow, zero side effects from a warned
  attempt, and edit-never-triggers. Also fixed test_application_edit.py's shared
  fixture (added confirm_duplicate=True default) since it intentionally creates
  same-company applications for unrelated reassignment tests.

  Full suite: 312 passed (285 + 27). Journal updated. Nothing committed.

✻ Churned for 6m 40s

● FR-002 Review

  I re-read FR-002's full requirement text, architecture.md's "Application
  Duplicate Detection" section (plus the "Transaction Boundaries" language
  governing when confirmations may run before vs. inside a transaction), and
  cross-checked test-strategy.md. I also verified several claims empirically
  rather than trusting my own summary from the implementation turn.

  Confirmed correct and compliant:
  - The matching rule exactly matches architecture.md's wording: company +
  external job ID when available (mutually exclusive with the job-title
  fallback, verified this edge case explicitly), company + job title otherwise.
  - No database uniqueness constraint was added on either indicator — confirmed
  via git diff on schema.sql (no changes), satisfying "neither shall be made
  unique on APPLICATION."
  - The duplicate check runs before any reference-data resolution and before any
  transaction opens, consistent with architecture.md's "normalization,
  validation, duplicate review... shall occur before committing changes" and "do
  not hold a database write transaction open while waiting for user
  confirmation." I verified the meaningful half of this (source-table
  protection) empirically: simulated a version of create_application that
  resolves the source before the duplicate check, and confirmed a warned attempt
  would then leak an orphan source row — the real implementation doesn't.
  - confirm_duplicate correctly allows the save to proceed despite a real match,
  satisfying "warn... rather than prevent" and "the database shall allow the
  confirmed application to be saved."
  - No SQL injection risk: the only string-interpolated SQL fragments
  (_NORMALIZE_SQL.format(expr=...)) are built from hardcoded column names, never
  from user input; all user-supplied values are passed as bound parameters.
  - Editing never triggers the check, correctly matching FR-002's "during
  application entry" scope and the interpretation already settled during FR-006.
  - Diff is cleanly scoped to FR-002 plus the one necessary test-fixture fix in
  test_application_edit.py — no scope creep into FR-004.

  Findings:

  1. Low/Medium — no explicit "Cancel" control on the create form, including in 
  the duplicate-warning state. FR-002 says "the user shall be able to review the
  potential duplicate and either cancel the new application or proceed with
  saving it." Currently "cancel" is only satisfied implicitly (navigate away
  without submitting) — there's no dedicated Cancel link, unlike every other
  confirmation/warning state in the app (edit's page-level Cancel link, the
  archive-confirm page's Cancel, the status-correct/delete pages' Cancel). This
  gap predates FR-002 — the original create-application slice never had a Cancel
  link and no prior review flagged it — so it's not a new regression, but
  FR-002 is the first requirement to use the word "cancel" in connection with
  this form, making the gap newly and specifically relevant, especially right
  when a user has just been told their entry might already exist.
  2. Low — one of two assertions in 
  test_duplicate_warned_attempt_creates_no_reference_data doesn't protect 
  anything. The test checks that a warned/unconfirmed attempt creates zero new
  company and zero new source rows. I verified the source assertion is genuinely
  protective (confirmed by simulation). The company assertion is tautologically
  true and can never fail: a duplicate match structurally requires the matched
  company to already exist, so that code path can never reach company creation
  regardless of implementation correctness. Not a functional defect — just a
  test that looks like it's checking two things but only meaningfully checks
  one.

  No High or Critical findings. Both are minor; I'd suggest fixing finding 1
  (add a Cancel link to the create form) since it's a real, if small,
  user-facing gap against explicit requirement wording. Finding 2 is cosmetic
  and not worth a dedicated fix on its own.

  Want me to fix either or both?

● Recommendation: FR-004 (Search and Filter Applications) next

  At this point FR-004 isn't really competing against other candidates — it's
  the only remaining major functional requirement. FR-001, FR-002, FR-003,
  FR-005 through FR-009 are all implemented; FR-010 (reference-data reuse) and
  FR-011 (validation) are cross-cutting concerns already substantially realized
  across every prior slice, with two small, independent known gaps (below)
  rather than unimplemented capabilities of their own scale. So the interesting
  question isn't "is FR-004 next" — it's "is FR-004 ready, and what does
  finishing it actually involve."

  Why it's ready now, and what it depends on

  FR-004 depends on FR-003 (the list view itself) and, more specifically, on
  FR-009's minimal record-state work, which was deliberately built as a subset
  of FR-004 rather than a parallel mechanism — list_applications already takes
  sort, direction, page, and record_state, and builds its WHERE/ORDER BY clauses
  from pre-validated, whitelisted SQL fragments combined with AND. That's
  exactly the shape FR-004 needs to extend: add more optional WHERE fragments
  (free-text substring match, category IN-lists, a date range) to the same
  query-building function, rather than writing a new one. This was explicitly
  designed for that extension at the time (per architecture.md: "Archived and
  All record-state filters expose historical applications using the same search,
  filter, sort, and pagination behavior").

  Nothing later in Phase 1 depends on FR-004 — it's a leaf feature like FR-002
  was, just larger. Finishing it effectively closes out Phase 1's functional
  scope.

  Decisions to resolve before implementation

  This is the largest remaining slice in terms of both UI surface and
  query-building complexity, so it's worth more up-front decisions than usual:

  1. Job location filter shape is genuinely ambiguous. FR-004 explicitly lists
  which filters support multi-select: "Status, source, work arrangement, and
  employment type filters shall support selection of multiple values" — job
  location is not in that list, despite being one of the six filter categories.
  It could mean job location is single-select, free-text, or simply an omission.
  I'd lean toward multi-select of the distinct job-location combinations 
  currently in use (for UI consistency with the other four, and because job
  locations are already normalized city/state/country combos with an established
  display format), but this needs an explicit decision before implementation,
  not an assumption.
  2. Free-text search implementation correctness. Substring matching means SQL
  LIKE, which requires escaping user-supplied % and _ wildcard characters (e.g.
  LIKE ? ESCAPE '\') — otherwise a literal search for "50%" behaves
  unpredictably. This isn't a security issue (values are still parameterized),
  but it's a correctness trap specific to this slice that hasn't come up before,
  worth calling out explicitly so it's not missed.
  3. UI mechanics for multi-select filters. No prior slice needed a multi-select
  control, and the project has a stated "minimal JavaScript" constraint. I'd
  recommend checkbox groups over native <select multiple> (more discoverable
  without JS, no ctrl/cmd-click affordance to explain) — a real UI decision, not
  just an implementation detail.
  4. What "clear filters" resets to. FR-004 says clearing "returns to the
  complete application list" — does that mean the default list (Active, no
  filters, default sort), or literally every application regardless of state
  (i.e., resets record state to All)? I'd interpret "complete application list"
  as FR-003/FR-009's already-established default (Active, unfiltered), but the
  text supports either reading and it should be settled explicitly.
  5. Date-range validation. Should a beginning date after the ending date be
  rejected as invalid, or simply allowed to return zero results naturally
  (consistent with the existing "no-results" philosophy)? Not specified by
  FR-004; I'd lean toward the latter (no new validation rule) unless there's a
  reason to add one.
  6. Query-string design for carrying criteria across 
  sort/pagination/record-state links. Every existing list-page link (sort
  headers, pagination, the record-state nav) currently round-trips
  sort/dir/page/state. FR-004 adds roughly seven more parameters (free-text
  query, five category filters, two date-range bounds) that all need to survive
  every one of those link clicks — a materially bigger template/URL-building
  surface than anything built so far, worth planning rather than discovering
  incrementally.

  Not recommended as part of this slice, but worth keeping visible

  Two small, independent gaps remain open from earlier reviews and don't
  naturally bundle with FR-004 (neither touches the list/search code): FR-011's
  "syntactically valid web URL when supplied" validation (deferred since the
  original create-application slice), and FR-010's "select an existing
  company/location/source" UI affordance (currently only satisfied at the
  data-normalization level, with plain free-text inputs). Both are small,
  targeted additions better handled as their own short follow-ups whenever
  convenient, not folded into FR-004.

  I have not modified or implemented anything. Let me know if you'd like me to
  proceed with FR-004 under a particular resolution of the six decisions above,
  or want to discuss any of them further first.

● Review of the six proposed decisions

  1. Job location is single-select. Sound, and better-grounded than I gave it
  credit for in my last turn. FR-004 explicitly names which filters get
  multi-select support — "Status, source, work arrangement, and employment type
  filters shall support selection of multiple values" — and job location is
  conspicuously absent from that list, alongside date range (which is a range,
  not a select, by nature). Reading that omission as deliberate rather than
  accidental is the more textually faithful interpretation. No contradiction.

  2. Free-text search uses literal substring matching with correct SQL escaping;
  no fuzzy matching. Matches architecture.md verbatim ("Search uses
  case-insensitive substring matching across company, job title, and external
  job ID") and FR-004's own text. Sound, no contradiction. Two details worth
  locking in now since they're easy to get wrong later: the three fields must
  combine with OR (a term matching any of company/job title/external job ID
  should surface the row — requiring all three would practically never match
  anything), and this inherits the same ASCII-only case-folding limitation
  already documented and accepted in ADR-0001 for normalized matching elsewhere
  — not a new gap, just consistent with existing precedent.

  3. Standard GET form, no JavaScript. Sound, and it's the right call for a
  second reason beyond the "minimal JavaScript" tech constraint: every existing
  list-page control (sort headers, pagination, the record-state nav) is already
  a plain GET <a href>. A GET-based filter form is the only choice consistent
  with that, and it directly enables decision 6 — the URL itself becomes the
  shareable/bookmarkable state, which a POST-based form would break. No
  contradiction; this decision reinforces the others rather than sitting
  independently.

  4. Clear Filters returns to the default Active, unfiltered list with default 
  sort. This resolves the ambiguity I flagged well — "the complete application
  list" is more consistent with FR-003's own definition of the default list
  (Active, application_date descending) than with "All" record state, since
  FR-003 establishes that phrase's meaning first and FR-004 doesn't redefine it.
  Sound, no contradiction. One thing to make explicit for implementation: this
  also resets page to 1 (not stated, but implied and worth writing down so it
  isn't missed).

  5. Invalid date-range input produces a validation error while preserving 
  entered criteria. Sound in principle, but needs one clarification and one
  genuinely new mechanical consideration:
  - Scope of "invalid." I'd fold in both malformed date syntax and
  beginning-date-after-ending-date, by direct analogy with the project's
  existing compensation min/max precedent (an explicit, required validation
  rule, not a "let it return zero results" situation). Worth confirming that's
  the intended scope, since the phrase "invalid date-range input" could be read
  either narrowly (syntax only) or broadly (including the logical ordering
  case).
  - This is a read-only GET request, not a write. Every prior "validation error,
  preserve entered values" case in this app was a POST-then-redisplay pattern.
  A search/filter page has no such distinction — every load is already a fresh,
  bookmarkable GET, and "preserving criteria" just falls out naturally from
  populating the inputs from request.args, the same way sort/page/state already
  do. The one real decision is what the results table shows while the error is
  displayed: I'd recommend rendering it empty (not attempting to apply a broken
  filter), with the error banner making clear why, distinct from a legitimate
  no-results state. Worth confirming, since it wasn't specified.

  6. Preserve all active criteria across list navigation. Sound and required,
  but "appropriately" hides a real mechanical detail worth pinning down now so
  it isn't half-implemented next session: the filter form's own submission must
  reset the page (by simply not carrying a hidden page field forward — a fresh
  GET submission naturally starts at page 1, which is exactly correct per
  FR-004's "changing search or filter criteria shall return to the first page"),
  while still carrying forward sort and state via hidden fields (since changing
  filters shouldn't disturb the current sort or record-state). Conversely, the
  sort/pagination/record-state links must each merge the currently active
  search/filter params into their own target URL without resetting them. No
  contradiction — just the one place where "preserve appropriately" needs to
  become concrete code-level behavior, and getting it backwards (e.g., a stray
  hidden page field on the filter form) is exactly the kind of bug that would
  slip through if not called out ahead of time.

  None of the six decisions are contradicted by requirements, architecture, or
  the existing implementation. All six are sound as stated, with the refinements
  above.

  ---
  Final agreed FR-004 implementation scope

  Query parameters (all on GET /applications, extending the existing
  sort/dir/page/state):
  - q — free-text search (trimmed; OR across company.name,
  application.job_title, application.external_job_id; case-insensitive substring
  via LIKE ... ESCAPE, with %, _, and the escape character itself escaped in
  the user's input before interpolation)
  - status, source, work_arrangement, employment_type — multi-value
  (request.args.getlist(...)), each combined with OR within the category,
  options sourced from: status (the STATUS table, existing _status_options
  pattern), work_arrangement/employment_type (existing
  WORK_ARRANGEMENTS/EMPLOYMENT_TYPES constants), source (distinct sources
  currently referenced by at least one application, to avoid offering options
  that can never match)
  - job_location — single value, holding a location_id (not an encoded display
  string — clean, unambiguous, and location rows are already deduplicated by the
  existing normalized-uniqueness index), populated from distinct location_id
  values currently used as application.job_location_id across all record states
  (not just the current one, so the option list doesn't shift confusingly when
  the record-state filter changes)
  - date_from, date_to — optional application_date bounds (ISO date strings,
  type="date" inputs)
  - All filter categories combine with AND; multiple values within a category
  combine with OR (per FR-004's example).

  Validation: a malformed date or a beginning date after the ending date
  produces a visible error (consistent styling with the existing #form-error
  pattern), entered criteria remain populated in the form (naturally, via
  request.args), and the results table renders empty rather than attempting to
  apply the broken filter.

  Clear Filters: a single control that navigates to /applications with no query
  parameters at all — i.e., Active record state, no search/filters, default sort
  (application_date descending), page 1.

  Navigation/state preservation mechanics:
  - The filter form is a method="get" form submitting q + the category/date
  fields, plus hidden sort and state fields (carrying forward the current sort
  and record state) — but no hidden page field, so submitting it naturally lands
  on page 1.
  - Sort headers, pagination links, and the record-state nav all continue to be
  plain <a href> GET links, each merging the currently active
  q/category/date-range values into their own target URL (a small Jinja
  helper/macro for "current args, override just this one" is worth building
  rather than hand-writing every url_for(...) call).
  - Sort-header clicks and record-state clicks continue to reset to page 1
  (already the existing behavior for both); pagination clicks do not reset page
  and continue to preserve sort/state as they already do.

  Empty/no-results states: distinguish "no applications recorded at all"
  (existing message) from "no applications match the active search/filter
  criteria" (new message, per FR-004), from "date-range validation error" (new,
  distinct from a legitimate no-results state).

  This should be sufficient for the next session to begin implementation
  directly without re-deriving any of this. No files were modified in this turn.

  Restated FR-004 decisions and scope

  1. Job location — single-select, backed by FR-004's explicit list of which
  four filters get multi-select (status, source, work arrangement, employment
  type) — job location's absence from that list is read as deliberate.
  2. Free-text search — literal substring, case-insensitive, properly escaped, 
  no fuzzy matching — OR across company/job title/external job ID, LIKE ... 
  ESCAPE with %, _, and the escape character itself escaped.
  3. Standard GET form, no JavaScript — consistent with every existing list-page
  control and required for decision 6 (URL-as-state).
  4. Clear Filters → Active, unfiltered, default sort, page 1.
  5. Invalid date range (malformed or beginning-after-ending) → visible 
  validation error, entered criteria preserved via request.args, results table 
  renders empty rather than applying a broken filter.
  6. All active criteria preserved across navigation — the filter form carries
  hidden sort/state fields but no hidden page (so submitting it naturally resets
  to page 1); sort/pagination/record-state links merge the currently active
  search/filter params into their own URLs without resetting them.

  Query params: q, status, source, work_arrangement, employment_type
  (multi-value), job_location (single location_id), date_from/date_to.

       894 +## 2026-09-21                                                
       895 +                                                             
       896 +### Search and Filter Applications                           
       897 +                                                             
       898 +- Implemented FR-004 ("Search and Filter Applications"): free
           +-text search                                                 
       899 +  across company/job title/external job ID, category filters 
           +(status,                                                     
       900 +  source, work arrangement, employment type, job location), a
           +nd an                                                        
       901 +  application-date range - all combined with the record-state
           + visibility                                                  
       902 +  already built for FR-009, via a `GET`-only, JavaScript-free
           + form on the                                                 
       903 +  existing application list page.                            
       904 +- Session continuity: this slice resumed from a prior session
           + that                                                        
       905 +  deliberately stopped after design-decision work rather than
           + risk leaving                                                
       906 +  FR-004 partially implemented. Before starting, re-read requ
           +irements,                                                    
       907 +  architecture, test strategy, the journal, and the six agree
           +d design                                                     
       908 +  decisions from that session's transcript (archived at      
       909 +  `docs/transcripts/2026-09-20-claude-code-session.txt`); con
           +firmed the                                                   
       910 +  repository, FR-002's commit, and all documentation matched 
           +exactly where                                                
       911 +  that session left off before beginning any implementation. 
       912 +- Pre-flight regression run surfaced one pre-existing, unrela
           +ted failure:                                                 
       913 +  `test_default_order_is_application_date_descending` hardcod
           +es                                                           
       914 +  `application_date="2026-09-20"` as a stand-in for "today" w
           +ith no                                                       
       915 +  explicit status effective time; once the real date moved pa
           +st that                                                      
       916 +  hardcoded value, `create_application` correctly required an
           + explicit                                                    
       917 +  effective time for what's now a retrospective date, and the
           + test's                                                      
       918 +  second application failed to create. This is a test-determi
           +nism defect                                                  
       919 +  (test-strategy.md requires "controlled or explicitly establ
           +ished"                                                       
       920 +  date/time values) that predates this slice and is unrelated
           + to both                                                     
       921 +  FR-002 and FR-004; left unfixed as out of scope, flagged ex
           +plicitly so it                                               
       922 +  isn't mistaken for something this slice introduced.        
       923 +- Applied the six agreed design decisions exactly as resolved
           + in the prior                                                
       924 +  session:                                                   
       925 +  1. Job location filter is single-select, keyed by `location
           +_id` (stable                                                 
       926 +     and unambiguous, unlike re-parsing a formatted display s
           +tring), backed                                               
       927 +     by FR-004's own text naming exactly four categories as m
           +ulti-select                                                  
       928 +     (status, source, work arrangement, employment type) - jo
           +b location's                                                 
       929 +     absence from that list was read as deliberate.          
       930 +  2. Free-text search is literal, case-insensitive substring 
           +matching,                                                    
       931 +     OR'd across company/job title/external job ID, with `%`/
           +`_`/the                                                      
       932 +     escape character itself escaped before building the `LIK
           +E ... ESCAPE`                                                
       933 +     pattern - verified directly with an injection-shaped sea
           +rch term and                                                 
       934 +     with literal `%`/`_` characters in stored data.         
       935 +  3. The filter UI is a standard `method="get"` form with no 
           +JavaScript,                                                  
       936 +     consistent with every existing list-page control already
           + being a                                                     
       937 +     plain GET link.                                         
       938 +  4. Clear Filters is a plain link to `/applications` with no
           + query                                                       
       939 +     parameters at all - Active, unfiltered, default sort, pa
           +ge 1 - reusing                                               
       940 +     FR-003's own definition of "the complete application lis
           +t" rather than                                               
       941 +     introducing a new one.                                  
       942 +  5. An invalid date range (malformed syntax, or a beginning 
           +date after the                                               
       943 +     end date) produces a visible error, preserves the entere
           +d raw values,                                                
       944 +     and shows zero rows rather than silently applying only t
           +he other,                                                    
       945 +     valid filters - an invalid range can't be honestly evalu
           +ated, so                                                     
       946 +     nothing is filtered by it.                              
       947 +  6. All active criteria are preserved across navigation: sor
           +t headers,                                                   
       948 +     pagination links, and the record-state nav all merge the
           + currently                                                   
       949 +     active search/filter values into their own URLs (via a `
           +filter_args`                                                 
       950 +     dict built once per request and spread into every `url_f
           +or()` call                                                   
       951 +     with Jinja's `**dict` syntax); the filter form itself ca
           +rries hidden                                                 
       952 +     `sort`/`state` fields but deliberately no hidden `page` 
           +field, so                                                    
       953 +     submitting it naturally lands on page 1, satisfying "cha
           +nging search                                                 
       954 +     or filter criteria shall return the application list to 
           +the first                                                    
       955 +     page" without any special-case logic.                   
       956 +- Extended `list_applications` rather than replacing it, per 
           +FR-009's own                                                 
       957 +  intent ("so FR-004 can extend this later rather than replac
           +e it"): the                                                  
       958 +  `FROM`/`JOIN` clause and column list were factored into sha
           +red                                                          
       959 +  `_LIST_FROM`/`_LIST_COLUMNS` constants reused by both the l
           +ist query and
