● FR-004 Review

  I re-read FR-004's full requirement text, architecture.md's list/search/filter
  guidance, and test-strategy.md, then checked the implementation against each
  clause — including direct empirical testing of the higher-risk areas (SQL
  construction, escaping, edge-case inputs) rather than just reading the code.

  Confirmed correct and compliant:
  - All seven filter dimensions from architecture.md are implemented (status,
  source, work arrangement, employment type, job location, date range, record
  state), each combining correctly: OR within a category (verified for status
  and work arrangement), AND across categories (verified with the exact worked
  example from FR-004's own text — SCREENING/INTERVIEWING OR'd, HYBRID/REMOTE
  OR'd, AND'd together).
  - Free-text search is case-insensitive substring matching, OR'd across
  company/job title/external job ID, with correct LIKE wildcard escaping —
  verified directly with literal % and _ characters in stored data and with a
  SQL-injection-shaped search term (parameterized throughout; no
  string-interpolated user input anywhere in the WHERE clause).
  - Record-state filtering (FR-009) continues to work identically under FR-004's
  filters — same query, same code path, per architecture's "same search,
  filter, sort, and pagination behavior."
  - Filters apply before sort/pagination (inherent to the SQL structure), and
  pagination/sort correctly narrow within the filtered set.
  - Clearing filters returns to FR-003's own definition of the default list; the
  "changing filters resets to page 1" requirement is satisfied structurally
  (the filter form has no hidden page field), and I confirmed the record-state
  nav correctly carries forward even an invalid date range so the error persists
  until fixed rather than silently vanishing.
  - FR-009's existing "No archived applications." wording is preserved exactly
  for a genuinely empty archived view; the new FR-004 message only appears when
  search/filter criteria are actually active.
  - No new database indexes were needed or missing per architecture's
  "personal-use scale" guidance — the existing idx_application_job_location_id
  already supports the new equality filter, and low-cardinality columns (work
  arrangement, employment type) don't benefit from indexing at this scale.

  Findings:

  1. Medium — reproducible 500 error from an oversized job_location value. I
  confirmed this directly: GET 
  /applications?job_location=999999999999999999999999999999 crashes with an
  unhandled OverflowError (SQLite integers are 64-bit; Python's
  arbitrary-precision int() parses the string fine, so the error only surfaces
  when the value is bound as a query parameter deep inside list_applications).
  This is the same class of defect the FR-005 detail-view review found and fixed
  for application_id (try/except OverflowError → treat as not-found), but the
  fix wasn't applied to this new filter. By contrast, I verified an oversized
  page value does not crash — it's protected incidentally by the existing
  page-clamping logic — so this is specific to job_location_id. No existing test
  exercises this input. The correct behavior is the same as elsewhere: treat an
  out-of-range ID as "can never match," not a server error.
  2. Low/Medium — asymmetric accessibility marking for date-range ordering 
  violations. When date_from is after date_to, I verified only the date_from
  input receives aria-invalid="true"; date_to does not, even though the
  violation is a relationship between both fields, not a defect in date_from
  alone. (The single-field malformed-syntax case correctly marks whichever field
  is actually malformed — this only affects the ordering-violation case.) No
  test covers aria-invalid behavior for either case.
  3. Low — verified-correct UI-state behaviors lack regression coverage. Two
  things I confirmed work correctly by hand but aren't protected by a test: (a)
  following "Clear Filters" actually resets all active criteria end-to-end (the
  existing test only checks the link's href attribute, not the result of
  visiting it); (b) the job-location <select>'s selected attribute correctly
  reflects the active filter on redisplay (only the functional filtering result
  is tested, not this visual reflection).

  No High/Critical findings — nothing causes data loss or incorrect results
  shown as correct; finding 1 is a crash on a deliberately-crafted URL, not
  something reachable through ordinary use of the UI.

  Want me to fix finding 1 (and optionally 2), matching the established pattern
  of closing out real defects before commit?

● Summary

  Root cause: test_default_order_is_application_date_descending posted its
  second application with a hardcoded application_date="2026-09-20" and no
  explicit initial_status_effective_at, silently relying on create_application's
  "APPLIED + application_date is today" shortcut to supply one. That reliance
  was never made explicit, and once the real date moved past 2026-09-20, the
  shortcut stopped applying — create_application correctly required an explicit
  effective time, the POST re-rendered the create form with a validation error
  instead of redirecting, and the second application was simply never created.
  No production defect; the test's own fixture setup was wall-clock-dependent in
  a way that violated test-strategy.md's requirement for "controlled or
  explicitly established" date/time values.

  Fix: replaced both dates with fixed, clearly-past values (2020-01-01 and
  2020-06-15), each with its own explicit initial_status_effective_at, removing
  any dependency on the real calendar entirely rather than swapping in a
  different date that would eventually fail the same way. No production code
  touched.

  Verified the fix is genuinely protective, not just passing trivially:
  temporarily patched LIST_DEFAULT_DIRECTION from "desc" to "asc" and confirmed
  the test correctly fails under that simulated regression before restoring it.

  Full suite: 363 tests, all passing — this was the last outstanding failure;
  the suite is now completely clean.

  Journal updated with a clearly separate "Test Maintenance" section,
  distinguished from the FR-004 entries above it, and the stale "stopping before
  review" note at the end of the FR-004 section was corrected to reflect that
  the independent review and fixes already completed.

  Nothing committed — both FR-004 and this test-maintenance fix are ready
  whenever you'd like to commit.

  condition" on validation failure. For compensation_min > compensation_max and
  "compensation provided without basis," the create/edit routes catch the
  resulting sqlite3.IntegrityError and show a fully generic message — "The 
  application could not be saved because it conflicts with existing data. Please
  review the values and try again." — that names neither the field nor the
  condition. This is inconsistent with every other validation path in the app,
  which is either field-specific (ValidationError + aria-invalid) or at least
  names the specific condition (e.g., the status-change duplicate-effective_at
  message, "another status change already has the same effective date and
  time"). error_field is never set for any IntegrityError anywhere in the app,
  so no field ever receives aria-invalid marking from this path.
  - No other inconsistencies found. Everything else I checked (status derivation
  consistency across list/detail/duplicate-detection, transaction boundaries,
  timestamp conventions, archive/restore semantics, record-state filtering)
  matches architecture.md precisely.

  Missing Regression Coverage

  - "Compensation basis required when compensation is present" has no service- 
  or route-level test.
  test_db.py::test_compensation_basis_required_when_compensation_present
  verifies the raw SQL CHECK constraint directly, but no test calls
  create_application/edit_application (or posts to the routes) with compensation
  and no basis to confirm the actual user-facing behavior. By contrast,
  compensation_min > compensation_max is covered at the service layer
  (test_database_constraint_failure_raises) and in test_application_edit.py.
  - Transaction-rollback verification is scoped only to create_application and 
  edit_application. change_application_status, correct_status_history,
  delete_status_history, archive_application, and restore_application all follow
  the identical commit/rollback pattern but have no dedicated rollback test,
  despite architecture.md explicitly naming "transaction rollback" as a
  testability target generally, not scoped to those two functions. Lower
  priority than the compensation gap — these are simpler, smaller-surface writes
  — but a real, named gap.
  - No other missing coverage found; FR-002/FR-004/FR-008/FR-009's own review
  cycles were unusually thorough (including empirical regression-test
  verification via monkeypatching), and that rigor is reflected in the current
  suite.

  Documentation Out of Sync

  - README.md is severely stale and internally duplicated. Its entire content
  (title through "Project Status") is repeated verbatim twice in the same file
  (lines 1–45 and 46–89 are identical — a real artifact/bug, not just
  staleness). Content-wise: it lists "FastAPI, PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy, REST
  APIs" under "Technology Direction" as if current, when the actual,
  long-since-decided Phase 1 stack is Flask + SQLite (per architecture.md and
  every implementation decision made). It states **Status:** Planning and
  "before application implementation begins," even though FR-001 through FR-009
  (minus the two FR-010/FR-011 gaps above) are fully implemented and tested.
  This is the most significant documentation gap — it's the first thing a reader
  (or reviewer) sees, and it actively misrepresents the project.
  - docs/lessons-learned.md exists but is empty (1 line), despite
  development-process.md's explicit call to "record lessons after they are
  observed." Numerous concrete lessons occurred over this project (the FR-001
  timezone/date-boundary bug, the whitespace/no-op-trigger bugs found during the
  persistence-foundation review, the FR-006 headquarters-carryover bug, several
  OverflowError findings, the wall-clock test-determinism failure) and are
  documented in the journal, but never distilled into this dedicated file. Lower
  priority — the journal already captures the substance — but a real, named gap
  against the process document.
  - product-vision.md and roadmap.md are not stale — both correctly frame
  PostgreSQL/FastAPI/REST APIs as long-term/Phase-2+ direction, consistent with
  the actual Flask/SQLite Phase 1 build.

  Recommended Minimum Work to Declare Phase 1 MVP Complete

  In priority order:

  1. Implement job-URL syntactic validation (FR-011). Small, well-scoped: a
  format check at entry time in create_application/edit_application, raising
  ValidationError for a non-URL value. This is the one clear "not implemented at
  all" functional gap.
  2. Add a CI workflow (.github/workflows/) running the existing pytest suite on
  push/PR, per test-strategy.md's explicit requirements. Low effort given
  pyproject.toml already defines everything needed (pip install -e .[dev],
  pytest).
  3. Fix README.md — remove the duplication, replace the stale
  FastAPI/PostgreSQL "current" tech section with the actual Flask/SQLite stack,
  and update "Status: Planning" to reflect the current implementation state.
  4. Add the compensation-basis-required regression test at the service/route
  level (small addition, mirrors the existing min>max test).
  5. Improve the compensation-relationship error message to name the condition
  (not necessarily the field) rather than the fully generic "conflicts with
  existing data" text — small, consistent with the pattern already used for
  status-change's duplicate-timestamp message.

  Lower priority, worth doing but not blocking a reasonable Phase 1 declaration:

  6. FR-010's reference-data "select existing" UI affordance (a real gap, but
  the largest remaining item in scope and effort — data-level correctness is
  already sound; this is a UX enhancement, not a correctness defect).
  7. Transaction-rollback tests for the five newer write paths.
  8. A lightweight requirements-coverage note (even a short table in the journal
  or a new short doc).
  9. Populate docs/lessons-learned.md from the journal's already-recorded
  incidents.

  Items 1–5 are small, concrete, and directly close functional/process gaps
  against explicit "shall" requirements. Item 6 is the one substantive remaining
  functional gap but is scoped as UX polish rather than a defect, and
  reasonably deferrable to a short follow-up if you want to declare Phase 1
  complete sooner. No files were modified in this audit.

● Summary

  What changed:
  - src/job_hub/applications.py: added _require_valid_url (stdlib
  urllib.parse.urlparse, restricted to http/https with a non-empty netloc, plus
  an explicit whitespace check since urlparse alone doesn't catch embedded
  spaces) and _require_compensation_basis (raises
  ValidationError("compensation_basis", ...)). Both wired into
  create_application and edit_application at the identical point their
  validation blocks already shared. No route changes needed — the existing
  generic ValidationError handling already surfaces error/error_field correctly.
  - _form_macros.html: added the missing {{ invalid('job_url') }} wiring — this
  field had no aria-invalid marking at all before, unlike every other validated
  field. Necessary for the new validation's error_field to be visible.
  - Database CHECK constraint for compensation-basis was left untouched —
  architecture.md calls for both layers, and the Python check is a second,
  earlier layer, not a replacement.

  Fallout fixed: two pre-existing tests created a javascript: job URL through
  the normal create path specifically to verify job_url_is_safe_link's
  display-time defense. That path no longer exists, so both were updated to
  inject the value via raw SQL instead — simulating legacy/bypass data, which is
  exactly what that property's defense-in-depth still protects against.

  Tests added: 50 new (12 function defs in test_applications.py, 8 in
  test_application_edit.py, 7 each in the two route test files), covering both
  create and edit paths, valid/invalid/blank/whitespace URL variants,
  min-only/max-only/both-without-basis, non-persistence on failure, aria-invalid
  marking, and that valid submissions still succeed. Verified genuinely
  protective by monkeypatching both validators to no-ops and confirming the
  pre-fix behavior (a stored dangerous URL; a generic IntegrityError instead of
  a field-attributed ValidationError) — exactly what the new tests assert
  against.

  Full suite: 413 passed, 0 failures.

  Ambiguities/decisions made:
  - Interpreted "web URL" as http/https only, matching the existing
  job_url_is_safe_link precedent — not stated explicitly in FR-011, but
  consistent with prior interpretation in this codebase.
  - Added the whitespace check beyond urlparse alone after discovering it during
  implementation ("http://exa mple.com" parses "successfully" with the space
  left in) — a real gap urlparse alone wouldn't have caught.

  Deliberately not touched: compensation_min > compensation_max's equally
  generic database-conflict message. The audit flagged it as the same class of
  issue, but this task scoped the fix specifically to the compensation-basis
  case — left as-is per the instruction not to expand scope.

  Journal updated. Nothing committed. Ready for independent pre-commit review.

● FR-010 implementation, testing, and journal update are complete. Here's the
  report:

  What changed

  Design decisions (documented in code comments and the journal):
  - Mechanism: native HTML5 <datalist>, not <select> or an admin screen —
  rejected <select> because it can't accept free-text new values without JS
  (breaking FR-010's "create in-workflow" requirement), and rejected an admin
  screen because architecture.md explicitly prohibits forcing a separate
  administration workflow.
  - Suggestion scope: all existing records, including "orphaned" ones no longer
  linked to any application — deliberately different from FR-004's "currently in
  use" filter-option scoping, since FR-010 needs reuse of previously-created
  values regardless of current linkage.

  Service layer (src/job_hub/applications.py): added list_all_company_names,
  list_all_source_names, list_location_component_options (+
  LocationComponentOptions dataclass).

  Routes (src/job_hub/routes.py): new_application and application_edit now pass
  these three option sets into their templates.

  Templates (_form_macros.html, new.html, edit.html): new
  reference_data_datalists() macro (5 <datalist> elements, rendered once per
  page since job-location and company-headquarters fieldsets share the same
  location datalists); list="..." attributes added to company_name, source_name,
  and the six location-component inputs.

  Tests added (25 new, all passing):
  - tests/test_reference_data_selection.py (new, 11 tests) — service-level
  coverage including empty-state, sorting, and orphaned-record inclusion for all
  three lookups.
  - tests/test_application_routes.py (+10) — datalist rendering, list="..."
  wiring, select-vs-new-value reuse, validation-error and duplicate-warning
  redisplay.
  - tests/test_application_edit_routes.py (+4) — same coverage for the edit
  form.

  I also verified the new tests are genuinely protective (not tautological) by
  temporarily stripping the datalist macro/attributes and confirming the
  relevant tests fail as expected, then restored the original file.

  No changes were made to validation, duplicate detection, or normalization
  logic — purely additive at the route/template layer.

  Test results

  No ambiguities or additional findings

  Nothing outside FR-010's scope was touched or discovered as newly broken.

● FR-010 Pre-Commit Review

  Sources re-read fresh this session: FR-010 (docs/mvp-requirements.md), the
  "Reference-Data Normalization and Reuse" and transaction sections of
  docs/architecture.md, docs/test-strategy.md, docs/development-process.md,
  ADR-0001 (docs/decisions/0001-phase-1-sqlite-persistence-foundation.md), the
  journal, and the complete working-tree diff (git diff --stat: 8 files, 489
  insertions, 0 deletions).

  Verification performed: full suite run twice (438 passed both times); mutation
  testing against a scratch copy of the working tree (not committed) — reverted
  list_all_company_names to FR-004-style "currently in use" scoping and
  confirmed the orphaned-record test fails as expected; stripped the list="..."
  attributes from _form_macros.html and confirmed both new wiring tests fail as
  expected; confirmed the repo diff was bit-for-bit restored after each mutation
  (git diff --stat unchanged).

  Findings

  Low — redundant test, no unique protective value
  tests/test_application_routes.py::test_post_selecting_existing_company_by_exac
  t_name_reuses_it (new) asserts the same outcome (company count stays 1) as the
  pre-existing test_post_reuses_existing_company_across_submissions in the same
  file — and the pre-existing test is actually stronger (it exercises a
  whitespace/case-normalized variant, not just an exact string match). The new
  test doesn't protect anything the old one doesn't already cover. Not harmful,
  just maintenance surface with no incremental coverage. Optional cleanup, not
  blocking.

  Informational — location datalist suggestions aren't deduplicated 
  per-component
  list_location_component_options runs SELECT DISTINCT 
  city/state_province/country independently per column. Two legitimately
  distinct location rows that differ only in case for one component (e.g.,
  "Austin, TX, USA" vs "austin, CA, USA") will surface as two separate
  autocomplete entries for that component. This doesn't violate FR-010 — the
  requirement's normalized-reuse clause is about full city+state+country
  triples, not independent components — but it's a minor characteristic worth

● 438 passed, 0 failures. File changes are exactly as intended.

  Summary

  Files changed:
  - .github/workflows/ci.yml (new) — the CI workflow
  - docs/journal/2026-09.md (modified) — audit reassessment + CI implementation
  entry

  What the workflow does:
  - Triggers on push and pull_request (unrestricted, per the requirement's
  literal wording)
  - Single test job on ubuntu-latest: checkout → setup-python@3.14 (matching
  pyproject.toml's requires-python) → pip install -e .[dev] → bare pytest
  - Relies on pyproject.toml's existing testpaths/pythonpath config, so pytest
  alone runs the entire unit/integration/Flask suite exactly as it's been run
  all session

  Key scope decisions (documented in the journal with rationale):
  - One job/one pytest step, not three separated by test level — the codebase
  has never split unit/integration/Flask tests via markers, and inventing that
  split now would be new tooling beyond what was asked.
  - No separate "isolated environment" step — GitHub-hosted runners are already
  fresh VMs, and every test already isolates its own SQLite DB via tmp_path, so
  there's nothing left to provision.
  - No coverage, linting, matrix builds, deployment, or Selenium/browser steps —
  all explicitly out of scope.

● Independent Pre-Commit Review: CI Workflow

  Re-read test-strategy.md's "Continuous Integration" section,
  development-process.md and roadmap.md (no additional CI requirements in
  either), pyproject.toml, and ADR-0001 (no CI-relevant content) fresh. Reviewed
  the complete working-tree diff (.github/workflows/ci.yml new,
  docs/journal/2026-09.md modified — confirmed nothing else touched).

  Critical — blocks commit as-is

  src/job_hub/schema.sql is gitignored and has never been committed. The CI 
  workflow will fail on every single run.

  db.py:7 reads SCHEMA_PATH = Path(__file__).parent / "schema.sql", and db.py:32
  calls SCHEMA_PATH.read_text() inside init_db(), which every test and every
  create_app() call depends on. .gitignore:32 has a blanket *.sql rule (intended
  for "Database dumps and local databases," alongside
  *.dump/*.sqlite/*.sqlite3), which unintentionally also matches
  src/job_hub/schema.sql — a source file the application needs at runtime, not a
  data dump. Confirmed with git status --ignored --short (!! 
  src/job_hub/schema.sql) and git log --all --oneline -- src/job_hub/schema.sql
  (empty — zero history, ever).

  I reproduced the exact failure mode: cloned the repository fresh into a
  scratch directory (what actions/checkout effectively does), applied this
  session's uncommitted .github/workflows/ci.yml, installed dependencies, and
  ran pytest — result: 5 failed, 1 passed, 432 errors, every one a
  FileNotFoundError on schema.sql. This is pre-existing repository state, not
  something this diff introduced, but it means the CI workflow being reviewed 
  cannot succeed on GitHub — every push and PR will show a hard red failure, for
  a reason unrelated to actual code correctness. I checked for sibling problems
  (any other Path(__file__)-relative runtime file, templates, static assets) —
  confirmed nothing else is affected; this is the one file.

  This must be resolved before or together with committing the workflow — either
  un-ignore and commit schema.sql specifically, or narrow the .gitignore *.sql
  pattern so it only matches actual dumps (e.g. /data/*.sql or similar) rather
  than every .sql file in the tree.

  Medium — validation methodology gap (the kind that produces false confidence)

  The journal claims the throwaway-venv test confirmed the commands "succeed
  exactly as the workflow will run them on a clean runner." That overstates what
  was actually verified. pip install -e .[dev] in a fresh venv only isolates
  Python package state — it still points at the existing, already-checked-out
  working directory, which has schema.sql physically present on disk despite
  being untracked. A venv-only test can never detect a tracked-vs-untracked-file
  gap like the one above; only a true fresh git clone (which is what caught it
  during this review) exercises the same code path actions/checkout uses. Worth
  correcting in the journal's framing, and worth adopting git clone-based
  validation as the standard local-CI-check method going forward rather than
  venv isolation alone.

  Everything else checked out clean

  - Triggers: on: push / pull_request, unrestricted — matches the requirement's
  literal "changes pushed to the repository and...pull requests."
  - Python version: "3.14" (correctly quoted, avoiding the classic YAML
  float-parsing gotcha) matches pyproject.toml's requires-python = ">=3.14".
  - Dependency install: pip install -e .[dev] — correct, matches local dev
  convention.
  - Test command: bare pytest correctly picks up pyproject.toml's
  testpaths/pythonpath config — verified directly (once schema.sql is present,
  all 438 tests pass in a fresh clone).
  - Fails on failure: independently verified by injecting a genuine assertion
  failure into a scratch copy — pytest exits 1, and GitHub Actions' default run:
  step behavior (no continue-on-error) turns that into a failed job/workflow
  with no extra config needed.
  - Scope: only checkout, setup-python, pip install, pytest — no coverage, lint,
  matrix, deploy, or Selenium/browser steps. Matches the instruction and
  test-strategy.md's repo split.
  - YAML validity: parses cleanly under PyYAML (noting the well-known, harmless
  on:-as-boolean YAML 1.1 quirk that doesn't affect GitHub's actual parser). I
  could not run actionlint for full schema validation — Docker is present but
  permission-denied in this sandbox, and npx/pip couldn't fetch a validator
  package without further access — disclosing this as a real limit of my own
  verification, not a defect found in the file.
  - Journal is otherwise accurate: file-change scope, test counts, and the
  FR/NFR reassessment content all check out against the diff and my own
  independent spot-checks.

  Verdict

  Not ready to commit. The workflow YAML itself is well-scoped and correctly
  designed, but it will fail immediately and permanently on GitHub due to the
  pre-existing schema.sql gitignore gap — a real, previously-undetected defect
  this review surfaced specifically because adding CI is what makes "fresh
  checkout" behavior matter for the first time. Recommend fixing the
  .gitignore/schema.sql tracking issue (either as part of this change or
  immediately alongside it) before committing the CI workflow, and tightening
  the journal's validation-methodology claim. No files were modified during this
  review.

  Independent Pre-Commit Review: FR-011 Compensation Min/Max Validation

  Re-read FR-011, architecture.md's data-constraints table and
  transaction-boundary section, and test-strategy.md fresh. Reviewed the
  complete diff (6 files, 323 insertions/11 deletions) and ran independent
  verification beyond what the implementation summary claimed.

  Findings

  Low — two new route-level tests don't discriminate the new behavior from 
  pre-existing protection

  test_post_compensation_min_exceeds_max_does_not_create_application and
  test_post_edit_compensation_min_exceeds_max_does_not_change_persisted_value
  assert "nothing was persisted," but I confirmed via mutation testing
  (neutering _require_compensation_range) that these two specifically still pass
  even with the new check disabled — the database's own CHECK constraint plus
  the existing generic IntegrityError catch-all already guaranteed
  non-persistence before this change. They're valid regression tests for a
  general property, just not specific to the new validation layer they're
  grouped under. Not harmful, but the journal's phrasing ("route layer... no
  application is created/changed on failure" as coverage of "the specific
  behavior") slightly overstates what's newly verified here.

  Low — "compensation_max" in body assertion is tautological

  In both new route-level "shows specific validation error" tests, assert 
  "compensation_max" in body is always true regardless of what the error message
  says — I confirmed the string "compensation_max" appears in the page even on
  a plain GET with no error at all, since the form always renders a
  compensation_max input (name="compensation_max", id="compensation_max"). This
  assertion gives the appearance of verifying message content but doesn't. It
  mirrors a pre-existing weak pattern already in the codebase
  (test_post_compensation_without_basis_shows_specific_validation_error's
  identical "compensation_basis" in body check has the same issue), so it's not
  a new category of mistake — but it's present in this diff and worth knowing
  about. The tests remain genuinely protective overall because of the adjacent
  aria-invalid="true" assertion, which I independently confirmed via mutation
  testing does correctly fail when the fix is disabled.

  Neither finding is blocking. If you want them tightened, the fix is narrow:
  scope the message-content check to the id="form-error" element specifically
  (e.g., assert the literal string "compensation_min: must not exceed 
  compensation_max" appears within the first ~150 chars after id="form-error"),
  and either drop or reframe the two non-discriminating "does not persist" tests
  as general regression coverage rather than new-behavior-specific.

  What checked out clean

  - Placement/transaction ordering: _require_compensation_range is called in
  both create_application (line 342) and edit_application (line 1114)
  immediately after _require_compensation_basis, before any write — the
  try:/write block starts after both checks in both functions. Matches
  architecture.md's "validation... shall occur before committing changes."
  - Boundary correctness: strict > comparison — compensation_min == 
  compensation_max is accepted, matching both FR-011's "shall not exceed"
  wording and the DB CHECK's <=. Verified directly (both new equal-value tests
  pass; DB constraint uses the same <=, no mismatch between layers).
  - Error field/message: ValidationError("compensation_min", "must not exceed 
  compensation_max") — confirmed via live HTTP request that the rendered banner
  reads exactly "compensation_min: must not exceed compensation_max",
  aria-invalid="true" is correctly placed only on compensation_min (not
  compensation_max), and this is a real, previously-existing template wire-up,
  not new.
  - DB constraint untouched: confirmed via git diff — no schema.sql changes.
  - Test fallout correctly handled: independently reproduced that
  compensation_min="not-a-number" genuinely reaches the database's STRICT-table
  rejection ("cannot store TEXT value in REAL column 
  application.compensation_min"), preserving the original intent of the two
  repurposed transaction-rollback tests rather than coincidentally passing for
  an unrelated reason.
  - Genuine protection, independently verified: neutered the fix myself (not
  just trusting the implementation's claim) and got 6 failures (not just the 4
  the summary mentioned — I also caught the two "raises before any writes"/"does
  not change persisted value" service-layer tests failing via wrong exception
  type), confirming these are real regression tests. Restored cleanly afterward
  (git diff --stat matched exactly).
  - No missed integration points: grepped for all
  compensation_min/compensation_max write sites — only the two already-covered
  INSERT/UPDATE statements in create_application/edit_application exist; no
  other write path (archive/restore, etc.) touches compensation.
  - Full suite: independently re-ran, 446 passed, 0 failures, matching the
  reported count exactly (438 baseline + 8 net new, arithmetic verified).

  counts, file list) check out against the diff and my independent testing. One
  minor wording imprecision (line ~1560 says "compensation_min named in the
  response body" where the code actually asserts on "compensation_max") —

  Medium — README's completion claim overstates coverage for NFR-004, and the 
  journal entry is internally self-contradictory about it

  README's Project Status section states: "All Phase 1 functional and 
  non-functional requirements defined in docs/mvp-requirements.md are 
  implemented, covered by an automated test suite, and verified through 
  continuous integration on GitHub Actions."

  This is not accurate for NFR-004 ("Phase 1 shall support the current
  Chromium-based browser..."). I confirmed via the journal itself (line 170,
  dated near the start of the project) that Chromium verification happened
  exactly once, manually, against the initial skeleton — never re-verified
  against the current full feature set, and there is no automated browser test
  anywhere in this repository (by design — that's job-search-hub-tests' job per
  the repo split, and that repository doesn't exist yet). CI runs pytest only;
  it verifies nothing about browser compatibility. So NFR-004 is neither
  "covered by an automated test suite" nor "verified through continuous
  integration" — the blanket "All... requirements... are implemented,
  covered..., and verified..." sentence is false for at least this one
  requirement.

  This traces to a real inconsistency in the journal entry itself: its opening
  bullet claims "Every FR-001 through FR-011 and NFR-001 through NFR-007 item 
  previously identified as partial is now resolved," but a later bullet in the
  same entry correctly lists NFR-004 among items still needing "a fresh Chromium
  smoke-check against the current full feature set." A reader trusting the
  summary line gets a false picture; a reader who continues to the
  deferred-items list gets the correct one. This is exactly the category of
  issue you asked me to check for ("no claims overstate Phase 1 completion").

  The distinction that got lost: your own audit report two turns ago correctly
  said "no BLOCKING work remains" — that's true and defensible. It got garbled
  into "every item is now resolved" when written into the journal, which is a
  stronger and inaccurate claim.

  Suggested fix (not applied): narrow both claims to what's actually true —
  e.g., README: "All Phase 1 functional and non-functional requirements are 
  implemented. The implementation is covered by an automated test suite verified
  through continuous integration; browser-level verification (NFR-004) is 
  tracked separately in docs/test-strategy.md and not yet automated." Journal:
  change the opening bullet to "Every item the prior audit classified as 
  required, blocking work is now resolved... NFR-004 remains explicitly 
  deferred, as detailed below," rather than claiming all NFR items are resolved.

  Low — same overclaim pattern, smaller scope, for FR-011's punctuation/quotes

  job-search-hub-tests hasn't been created — a reader could reasonably infer it

  Failing test: tests/test_application_archive_routes.py::test_post_archive_reco
  rds_archived_at_close_to_the_request_time

  assert datetime.datetime(2026, 9, 23, 16, 17, 2, 179106, tzinfo=utc) <=
  datetime.datetime(2026, 9, 23, 16, 17, 2, 179000, tzinfo=utc)

  Root cause (from the log, no code changes needed to diagnose): the test
  captures before = datetime.now(timezone.utc) at microsecond precision, then
  compares it against archived_at as persisted and read back from the database —
  but the database stores timestamps at millisecond precision
  (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.sssZ'), truncating rather than rounding). In this
  run, the real write happened at ...179106 microseconds; SQLite truncated that
  down to ...179000 (179 ms) when storing it, landing before the Python-side
  before timestamp was captured. The assertion before <= archived_at then fails
  by 106 microseconds — a timing-precision race in the test's own boundary
  comparison, not a functional defect.

  This is unrelated to the pushed commit. 3d4290d touched only README.md and
  docs/journal/2026-09.md — no application, test, or schema code changed. This
  is a pre-existing, timing-sensitive test that flaked on this particular run
  due to natural millisecond-boundary timing, not a regression introduced by the
  documentation correction.

  Per your instruction, I'm stopping here and making no changes. Local main is
  at 3d4290d (already pushed); nothing further has been touched.

● Summary

  Root cause: ADR-0001 deliberately documents millisecond persistence precision
  for all timestamp columns (SQLite's strftime('%f')). I confirmed empirically
  (2000 trials) that this truncates rather than rounds — the persisted
  archived_at can land up to ~1ms below a Python-side before bound captured with
  microsecond precision, even though the real write happened after before. This
  is a representation-precision artifact, not a timing bug: the test normally
  passes only because HTTP request overhead usually exceeds that ~1ms window,
  and the CI failure was a rare case where it didn't. No application defect —
  the persistence layer behaves exactly as ADR-0001 specifies.

  Files changed:
  - tests/test_application_archive_routes.py — added timedelta to the import;
  widened the assertion from before <= archived_at <= after to before - 
  tolerance <= archived_at <= after + tolerance with tolerance = 
  timedelta(milliseconds=1), matching the documented storage precision exactly.
  No production code, schema, or other test files touched.
  - docs/journal/2026-09.md — new entry recording the CI-discovered flake, root
  cause, investigation method, fix, and verification.

  Other tests checked: grepped the full suite for datetime.now(timezone.utc) and
  for any other parsed-persisted-timestamp-vs-wall-clock comparisons — this
  exact pattern exists in exactly one place. No other tests needed the fix.

  Verification:
  - 50 consecutive runs of the corrected test: 50/50 passed (previously
  intermittently failing on CI).
  - Targeted file: 26/26 passed. Full suite: 446 passed, 0 failures.
  - Negative/mutation check: overwrote archived_at via raw SQL to a value 10
  seconds before the real request window (simulating a genuine defect) and
  confirmed the corrected assertion still fails as expected — proving the 1ms
  tolerance doesn't mask real timing bugs, only the sub-millisecond truncation
  artifact.
  - (One scratch reproduction of the original flake via repeated subprocess runs
  timed out mid-loop and was cleanly reverted from a backup before restoring
  the real fix — git diff --stat confirms only the intended two-file change
  remains.)

● Independent Pre-Commit Review: CI Flake Fix

  Re-read ADR-0001's "Timestamp convention" section and architecture.md's
  "Timestamp Convention" / testability sections fresh. Inspected the complete
  diff directly (git diff) rather than the implementation summary — confirmed
  exactly two files changed: tests/test_application_archive_routes.py and
  docs/journal/2026-09.md.

  Findings

  Medium — the root-cause explanation misattributes the truncation mechanism, in
  both the test comment and the journal

  Both the new test comment and the journal entry state the flake is caused by
  "SQLite's strftime('%f') truncates... to the millisecond." I traced the actual
  code path for archived_at and found this isn't what happens here. routes.py's
  archive route calls archive_application(connection, application_id) with no
  now argument, so inside archive_application, now = now or 
  datetime.now(timezone.utc) captures the instant in Python, which is then
  formatted by _format_timestamp — value.strftime(...) + f"{value.microsecond //
  1000:03d}Z" — a Python-side integer floor-division truncation, not a SQL
  strftime() call. I confirmed via schema.sql that archived_at TEXT has no
  DEFAULT (strftime(...)) clause at all (unlike created_at/last_updated_at,
  which genuinely do use SQL-side strftime defaults) — so the SQLite-strftime
  explanation doesn't correspond to anything in this column's actual write path.

  I verified the real mechanism directly against _format_timestamp itself (3000
  trials): min(_format_timestamp(now) - now) = -0.999ms, max = 0.0ms —
  confirming Python's microsecond // 1000 produces mathematically identical
  truncation-only behavior (never rounds up, max ~1ms loss) to what the journal
  measured against raw SQLite strftime. The fix's magnitude, direction, and 
  justification are unaffected and remain fully correct — this is a factual
  misattribution in the explanation, not a flaw in the fix. But since the user
  explicitly asked me to verify the journal "accurately describes... root
  cause," and the same inaccurate claim is baked into the test's own code
  comment (which future maintainers will read directly at the assertion), I'm
  flagging this as a real, specific inaccuracy worth correcting before commit:
  attribute the truncation to _format_timestamp's microsecond // 1000 (used for
  archived_at), not SQLite's strftime('%f') (which governs
  created_at/last_updated_at instead).

  What checked out clean, independently verified

  - 1ms tolerance is not arbitrary: re-read ADR-0001 fresh — "millisecond
  precision" (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ) is an explicit, deliberate,
  already-accepted architectural decision, not an oversight. I independently
  measured the real truncation mechanism (_format_timestamp, 3000 trials): max
  deviation -0.999ms, never positive — 1ms is the tight, mathematically correct
  bound implied by flooring to millisecond granularity, not a padded/guessed
  value.
  - Symmetric application (both before and after sides) is justified, not just 
  defensive padding: I confirmed the upper bound (archived_at <= after) was
  never violated in any of my ~5000 combined trials across two independent
  measurements — but ADR-0001 documents granularity, not a specific rounding
  direction, so treating the contract symmetrically (rather than hard-coding an
  assumption about truncation direction that isn't part of the documented
  contract) is the technically correct, principled choice.
  - Detection capability preserved: independently constructed mutation tests at
  10ms, 100ms, and 1000ms simulated offsets — all correctly caught by the
  corrected assertion. (My own finer-grained sub-2ms mutation probes were
  confounded by my own test harness reintroducing the same
  millisecond-truncation artifact I was testing around — not a flaw in the
  production fix, just a methodological wrinkle in my verification script at
  that specific boundary; the practically meaningful magnitudes, representative
  of this project's own real historical timing bugs like the earlier UTC/local
  timezone defect, are unambiguously caught.)
  - No application defect masked: archive_application's now default correctly
  uses datetime.now(timezone.utc) (UTC-aware from the start, no local/UTC
  ambiguity); schema.sql's archived_at TEXT column and _format_timestamp behave
  exactly as ADR-0001 documents. No production code was touched by this diff —
  confirmed via git diff.
  - No other tests share this defect: independently grepped the full suite for
  datetime.now(, strptime, and before...after-style wall-clock window assertions
  — this pattern exists in exactly one place, matching the journal's claim
  exactly.
  - Only the intended files changed: confirmed via git status --short and full
  git diff — tests/test_application_archive_routes.py (import + widened
  assertion + comment) and docs/journal/2026-09.md only.
  - Test stability: independently re-ran the corrected test 40 consecutive times
  (0 failures) and the full suite (446 passed, 0 failures).

  Verdict

  Not quite ready to commit as-is. The fix itself is sound, tightly justified,
  non-arbitrary, and doesn't mask any application defect — all independently
  re-verified against the actual code path rather than trusting the summary. The
  one Medium finding is narrow and mechanical: correct "SQLite's
  strftime('%f')" to _format_timestamp's microsecond // 1000 truncation in both
  the test's code comment and the journal entry, since that's the mechanism
  actually operating in this test's code path. No other changes needed.

  Where the rules were incorporated, and why

  Everything was added to the existing "Source Control" section — no new
  top-level section was created. That section already owned commit-related
  guidance ("Changes should be committed in logical increments with descriptive
  commit messages"), and every rule requested is fundamentally about git
  mechanics, so extending it kept the addition co-located with the topic it
  belongs to rather than introducing a second place to look for commit rules.

  Specifically:

  - The normal workflow (implement → verify → independent review → address/defer
  findings → commit → push → verify CI) is stated as one explicit ordered
  sentence. It deliberately doesn't restate what "implement," "review," or
  "test" mean — those are already defined by the existing "Development Model"
  (steps 6–9) and "Testing and Verification" sections — it only adds what was
  missing: the concrete sequence terminating in commit/push/CI, which nothing in
  the document previously described.
  - Commit messages must be explicit/deliberate and human-specified, not 
  AI-invented — a new paragraph, since no prior guidance touched commit-message
  authorship at all.
  - Commit messages should be concise, imperative, purpose-focused — same
  paragraph, immediately following the authorship rule.
  - Independent review before committing, with findings addressed or 
  deliberately deferred — folded into the workflow sentence plus a following
  sentence, using "independent review" and "independent verification" language
  that already exists in the document's own Purpose statement (line 9), rather
  than inventing new terminology.
  - Push and CI verification are separate from committing; a local commit isn't 
  completion — its own paragraph, with a cross-reference to test-strategy.md
  (which owns CI requirements) formatted as [the test 
  strategy](test-strategy.md), matching the one existing precedent for
  cross-document links in this doc family (architecture.md's [the MVP 
  requirements](mvp-requirements.md)).

  "Development Model," "Testing and Verification," and "Definition of Done" were
  left untouched — the new content operationalizes what those sections already
  establish in the abstract, at the specific commit granularity, without
  duplicating them.

● Assessment

  Yes — the newly added text (still uncommitted) should be split. What I wrote
  treats this discipline as a git rule, but re-reading it against what was
  actually practiced this session, most of it isn't about git at all.
  Independent review, deliberate deferral, per-step authorization, stopping at
  the requested boundary, and failure handling all governed non-git moments too
  — e.g., "implement X, stop, don't commit," "if CI fails, report and don't
  fix," "run this specific test, not the whole suite" — none of which involve
  source control. Confining that discipline to "Source Control" would make it
  invisible to anyone consulting the document for a task that never reaches a
  commit.

  Recommended structure: one new top-level section, Source Control trimmed to 
  what's genuinely git-specific

  New section — something like ## AI-Assisted Change Control, placed after Human
  Direction and Review and before Implementation Instructions. That placement
  matters: it sits right after the section establishing who decides what, and
  right before the sections describing how a task is briefed, tested, and
  committed — it's the connective procedural layer between "humans own these
  decisions" and "here's how each topic-specific stage works."

  Content (to be drafted, not now):
  1. Implementation authorization — work proceeds from an explicitly scoped
  task; implementation should not extend beyond that scope without separate
  authorization. (Currently undocumented anywhere.)
  2. Verification — an implemented change is verified before being considered
  ready for review. Cross-reference Testing and Verification for what
  verification entails; don't restate it.
  3. Independent review before commit — should occur whenever practical,
  generalized from "before committing" to "before the change is considered ready
  to proceed."
  4. Findings addressed or deliberately deferred — not silently dropped. Worth
  naming explicitly, since it's slightly more specific than the phrase suggests:
  findings were consistently reported by severity, and unrequested fixes — even
  for things found — were not applied without asking. That nuance is real and
  recurring; it belongs here if this section gets drafted.
  5. Separate authorization per escalating step — committing, pushing, verifying
  CI, and any other action with effects beyond the local working copy each
  require their own explicit authorization; finishing one step never implies
  authorization for the next.
  6. Stopping at the requested boundary — status is reported and further
  direction awaited, rather than proceeding on inferred next steps. (Currently
  undocumented anywhere — a real gap.)
  7. Failure handling — unexpected test or CI failures are reported for a
  decision, not autonomously corrected, unless correction is itself the
  authorized task. (Currently undocumented anywhere — a real gap.)
  8. Journal traceability — each unit of work concludes with a journal entry.
  Cross-reference Documentation for what the journal should contain; don't
  restate it.

  Source Control, trimmed back: keep the existing "logical increments" sentence
  unchanged. Keep the commit-message rules (concise/imperative/purpose-focused,
  and "specified by human direction, not invented by an AI assistant") as
  concrete, git-specific rules a reader can find without reading the whole
  document — but they become instances of the new section's general
  authorization principle rather than a freestanding rationale. Replace the full
  workflow sequence and the "pushing/CI are separate" paragraph with a short
  pointer back to the new section, keeping only the CI cross-reference to
  test-strategy.md (that one's genuinely about CI's technical requirements, not
  authorization).

  Unchanged: Development Model, Testing and Verification, Definition of Done,
  Documentation, AI-Assisted Engineering. Each already covers its own topic at
  the right level of abstraction; the new section operationalizes them at the
  task-execution level without restating any of them.

  Still undocumented even after this restructuring

  - Destructive git operations require explicit authorization (force-push, hard
  reset, discarding uncommitted work, etc.). This was a hard constraint all
  session but currently exists only at the harness/system-prompt level — nothing
  in development-process.md reflects it, and it's exactly the kind of operating
  rule this document exists to capture.
  - Verifying a regression test is genuinely protective (reintroducing the
  defect and confirming the test fails, before trusting it) — now captured
  retrospectively in lessons-learned.md, but not established anywhere as a
  forward-looking standing practice in Testing and Verification. Outside the
  user's listed scope for this task, but worth flagging since it's a real,
  recurring Phase-1 discipline with nowhere to live yet.

  No files were modified. Ready to draft the actual section text and the trimmed
  Source Control revision on your go-ahead.

❯ Review the current project operating rules in docs/development-process.md,    
  along with the relevant project documentation and journal entries from this   
  Phase 1 effort, and incorporate the remaining operating practices established 
  during this session.                                                          
  The goal is not to append another isolated set of rules. First determine what 
  is already documented, then make the smallest coherent changes necessary so   
  the project's operating model covers all of the following without             
  duplication, contradiction, or unnecessary repetition.                        
  Authorization and confirmation                                                
  - Routine, non-destructive, in-scope operations may proceed without repeated  
  human confirmation when they are reasonably necessary to complete an          
  explicitly authorized task. Examples include reading/searching files,         
  inspecting Git status/diffs/history, running tests and verification commands, 
  comparing files, performing analysis, and other reversible local              
  investigation.                                                                
  - Do not repeatedly request confirmation for individual routine commands when 
  the overall task has already been authorized.                                 
  - Human approval remains required at meaningful control boundaries,           
  including:                                                                    
    - expanding beyond the authorized task scope;                               
    - committing changes;                                                       
    - pushing changes;                                                          
    - initiating CI or other externally consequential operations when not       
  already explicitly authorized;                                                
    - destructive Git operations such as force-push, history rewriting, hard    
  reset, or discarding uncommitted work;                                        
    - deleting, replacing, or intentionally discarding source/project records;  
    - proceeding with unrelated corrective work discovered during the           
  authorized task.                                                              
  - Completion or authorization of one operational stage does not imply         
  authorization for the next stage.                                             
  - Stop at the explicitly requested boundary, report status, and await human

● Summary

  Classification results (before editing)

  Most commit-workflow, authorization-boundary, independent-review, and
  failure-handling concepts from your list were already documented from the two
  prior restructuring passes. Six genuine gaps were found and closed; everything
  else was reinforced in place or left untouched.

  Rules added or changed, and why

  1. New paragraph: routine operations don't need repeated confirmation. Nothing
  previously said this — every existing sentence stated what does need
  approval. Scoped deliberately: the example list (reading/searching, git 
  status/diff/log, running tests, comparing files) is entirely read-only, and
  the catch-all says "reversible local investigation," not "reversible
  operations," so it can't be stretched to cover file edits.
  2. Control boundaries consolidated into one explicit list, adding two
  previously-unnamed items: deleting/replacing/discarding source or project 
  records (distinct from Git-specific destructive operations) and proceeding 
  with unrelated corrective work discovered during a task. The existing "not
  performed as an incidental part of another task" nuance was extended to cover
  the new record-deletion item too.
  3. Independent review now explicitly excludes "prior narrative" (not just "own
  summary"), names requirements/architecture/ADRs as governing-documentation
  examples, and states findings must not disappear across later review
  iterations — directly reflecting the FR-004-citation correction from two turns
  ago.
  4. Failure handling expanded: failures must not be assumed caused by the
  current change; investigation should distinguish regression from pre-existing
  defect/flaky test/environmental/precision issue (the exact archived_at flake
  pattern); investigation authorization ≠ correction authorization; out-of-scope
  correction stops for direction; an authorized correction is followed by
  re-running verification.
  5. Journal entries now have an explicit evidentiary standard ("enough evidence
  to reconstruct what occurred... and how conclusions were verified") —
  describing what entries have actually contained all along.
  6. New ## Transcript Preservation and Provenance section (placed after
